Lacan connects that gap with the lack in jouissance and with the function of desire. Analysis, on his account, does not reveal that liberation lies in simply going beyond prohibition. Speaking around a limit is not the same as crossing it.

### Surplus-jouissance and Marx's surplus value

Lacan makes the Marx reference explicit on printed p. 20. The `a` functioning as surplus-jouissance is set alongside Marx's discovery of surplus value. He is careful not to claim that Marx invented surplus value out of nothing. Surplus labour existed before Marx, but Marx located its structural place. In Lacan's analogy, analytic discourse similarly enables object `a` to be recognised as functioning at the level of surplus-jouissance.

The analogy is formal rather than a claim that psychic life is reducible to political economy. What matters is the place of an excess produced within a structure. The surplus is not simply a treasure that can be accumulated without consequence. Lacan remarks that if one "pays" in jouissance and thereby has it, there is an urgency to squander it. He leaves this point suspended for later development.

### The four radical discourses

The fourth numbered movement names the four-footed apparatus as a device capable of defining four radical discourses. Lacan begins with the arrangement that he calls the master's discourse. He indicates that the historical importance of this discourse will be central to the year and connects it to the long philosophical treatment of mastery, with Hegel as an especially explicit instance.

He also names two of the other rotations directly. The second formula on the board is the hysteric's discourse. One of the remaining forms is the analyst's discourse. Lacan withholds the name of the fourth at this point, saying that naming it immediately would generate too many misunderstandings. Later in the seminar this fourth form is university discourse. In Chapter I, however, the important point is the production of the four structures through rotation rather than a completed commentary on each one.

The discourse formulas should therefore be read as social and signifying structures. Lacan does not present them as four temperaments, personality styles, professions, or institutions populated by four kinds of people. Terms move through four places; the discourse is defined by the arrangement and relation of positions.

### Master signifier, slave knowledge, and philosophy's extraction of savoir-faire

To ground why the first formula is the master's discourse, Lacan assigns `S1` to the signifier function on which mastery relies and `S2` to the field of the slave's knowledge. His discussion of Antiquity, including Aristotle's *Politics*, treats the slave not merely as a modern socioeconomic class category but as a function situated within household and political organisation. The slave is the bearer of *savoir-faire*, practical know-how.

This know-how is not mute animal adaptation. It is articulated enough to be transmissible. Precisely because it can be transmitted, it can be detached from the slave and appropriated by the master. Lacan describes the philosophical construction of *episteme* as an operation that finds the position from which this practical knowledge can be converted into the master's knowledge. The techniques of craftsmen or serfs are abstracted into transmissible, articulated knowledge.

Plato's *Meno* provides Lacan with his sharp example. The slave is questioned about a geometrical problem involving the square root of two and incommensurability. Conventional philosophical interpretation treats the episode as demonstrating knowledge already present in the slave. Lacan shifts the emphasis. The questions are master's questions; they prescribe the path of the response. The scene both acknowledges that the slave knows and dispossesses him of the function of his knowledge by reorganising it within another discourse. Philosophy, in this account, performs an extraction or transmutation of the slave's know-how into knowledge usable by the master.

This operation also clarifies why the relation between mastery and jouissance cannot be settled by saying that the master simply enjoys while the slave works. Lacan announces that the slave's position in relation to jouissance will require further articulation. The received image of enjoyment as the master's privilege does not adequately describe the structure.

### Episteme, science, Descartes, and the desire to know

Lacan distinguishes the philosophical operation that produces *episteme* from the emergence of modern science. Science is not merely the final accumulation of the master's theoretical knowledge. Aristotle's *theoria* belongs to the earlier philosophical formation. A different turn occurs when the subject is extracted from the strict `S1`-`S2` relation. Lacan names Descartes as the decisive figure for this operation and associates it with the birth of science.

The distinction matters because the history of knowledge is not a smooth progression. There is the earlier movement in which the master's discourse appropriates and formalises the slave's knowledge, and there is a later recommencement in which the functions supported by signifying articulation are rearranged. Lacan signals that this later transformation will become a major issue in the seminar.

At one limit of philosophy stands Hegel and the project of absolute knowledge. Lacan treats this as an extreme form of philosophy's service to the master, not as the final truth of knowledge. This prepares the chapter's closing distinction between knowledge and the desire to know.

Psychoanalysis, Lacan insists, gives no warrant for identifying desire for knowledge with the production of knowledge. A real master, in his provocative formulation, does not fundamentally want to know. The master wants things to work. This raises the historical question of how philosophy could have produced, or attributed to the master, a desire to know. Lacan does not answer it fully here. Instead he indicates another discourse, the hysteric's discourse, as the structure that leads to the production of knowledge. The distinction has consequences for pedagogy because the motive "wanting to know" cannot simply be assumed to be the cause of knowledge.

The main session closes on this unresolved provocation and is dated 26 November 1969.

### Supplement: "Following session: Agitation"

Source location: Chapter I supplement, printed pp. 24-26; session dated 10 December 1969.

The supplement turns an immediate institutional disturbance into another test of the discourse framework. Lacan says that people close to him had warned him that "agitation" was in the air. He replies that agitation interests him precisely because it may prove or disprove what he is claiming about discourse. The point is not to separate a pure doctrine from noisy historical circumstances. The circumstances themselves can show how a discourse takes effect.

Lacan reflects on his use of the first person. If he says "I", it is because he is looking at the discourse from somewhere else, from a place in which he is already situated by another discourse of which he is an effect. Saying that a discourse situates him and saying that the discourse is situated are closely connected. His teaching is therefore not represented as the sovereign expression of a self standing outside discourse.

He refers to a recent visit to Vincennes where obstruction had been expected because of his public prominence. He treats the incident as unsurprising. The more important point is the long history of institutional discomfort surrounding his audiences and teaching. At Sainte-Anne, his listeners had been periodically investigated to determine whether his teaching met the requirements of medical instruction. Lacan mocks the possibility that being "medical" would require ritual reference to accepted doctrines, such as presumed endocrine causes of neurosis or constitutional factors. Because he refused these gestures of institutional deference, the authorities were left confronting a teaching located in a medical setting but not conforming to their image of medical teaching.

He then recalls the social suspicion directed at his audiences. In reporting this historical judgement, Lacan mentions that their style, appearance, and manner were read by observers as signs of drug addiction and homosexuality. The point of the passage is not a clinical classification of the audience. It is the way institutional observers interpreted a group by its visible style and how the composition of an audience itself became a source of discomfort for the hosting institution.

The same dynamic continued at the Ecole normale superieure. Lacan characterises the Normaliens as university elites who know that one need not know something in order to teach it. The ordinary fact of smoking in his seminar became institutionally consequential because smoke penetrated into the space above, creating conflict with those occupying it. The episode illustrates his broader claim that apparently marginal material conditions can reveal the effects and boundaries of a discourse.

The supplement ends performatively. A building supervisor arrives during the session, then turns off the lights and retracts the blackboard. Lacan comments on the interruption, says that the events are taking place in a zone that has not lost its meaning, and declares the session over. The printed date is 10 December 1969. The interruption itself thus becomes part of the recorded seminar rather than an irrelevant disturbance removed from the conceptual record.

### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter I, "Production of the four discourses", printed pp. 11-26, including the session dated 26 November 1969 and the supplement "Following session: Agitation" dated 10 December 1969.

## AXES OF THE ANALYTIC SUBVERSION

### II. The master and the hysteric

Source location: Jacques Lacan, Seminar XVII, Chapter II, printed pp. 29-38. Session dated 17 December 1969.

#### The four discourse formulas as a reference grid

Lacan begins by placing all four discourse formulas in view as a working reference. The four structures use the same four terms, but each quarter-turn changes which term occupies the upper-left, upper-right, lower-left, and lower-right positions. The formulas are not four psychological types and not descriptions of four kinds of persons. They are formal arrangements that specify how a discourse is ordered.

```text
UNIVERSITY (U)          MASTER (M)

   S2  ->  a              S1  ->  S2
   --      --              --      --
   S1      $               $       a

HYSTERIC (H)            ANALYST (A)

   $   ->  S1              a   ->  $
   --      --              --      --
   a       S2              S2      S1
```

The starting point remains the definition of the signifier as what represents a subject for another signifier. The movement from one discourse to another is therefore not a change of vocabulary but a change in the structural place occupied by `S1`, `S2`, `$`, and `a`.

#### Knowledge that is not necessarily known

Lacan opens the chapter by challenging the apparently obvious assumption that knowledge must be known as knowledge. Psychoanalytic experience shows another order of knowledge, *savoir*, whose decisive feature is its articulation in signifiers rather than its possession by a conscious subject. The elementary relation `S1-S2` already permits a form of knowledge that is operative without being recognized as such.

This claim lets Lacan reread biography, historical destiny, and the unconscious. A life may believe that it knows what it is doing, what it has chosen, or where it is going, while an unconscious knowledge is nevertheless at work in the sequence of its acts and detours. From the point of view of the master's discourse, this invisible work is associated with the slave. The slave's labor carries and elaborates knowledge without making that knowledge present as a consciously totalized system.

Psychoanalysis therefore places knowledge itself in question. The issue is not merely to add new contents to an already closed encyclopedia. The analytic discovery undermines the image of knowledge as a completed whole that could in principle be possessed. Lacan briefly recalls skepticism to underline how weak an effect philosophical doubt has had on the political attraction of totality. The idea of a closed whole, supported by the body's imaginary form and by fantasies of complete satisfaction, continues to support political and epistemic constructions even after skepticism has formally challenged certainty.

#### The modern master and the transfer of knowledge

Lacan then returns to the historical transformation of the master's discourse. Marx's analysis of class struggle has not abolished the persistence of mastery. What changes is the place of knowledge. In the classical master's discourse, knowledge is on the side of the slave. In the modern configuration, Lacan associates the rise of an all-knowing `S2` in the dominant position with bureaucracy and with a new tyranny of knowledge.

The proletarian is described as dispossessed, but Lacan's emphasis is not simply juridical ownership. Capitalist exploitation frustrates the worker of his knowledge by rendering the worker's know-how subordinated to a knowledge that has been detached from him and installed elsewhere. Revolutionary restitution does not automatically return the worker's own knowledge. It can return another master's knowledge and therefore produce a change of masters rather than the disappearance of mastery.

The structural kernel of mastery remains that the master does not know what he wants. The slave, by contrast, knows something about the master's desire because the slave must anticipate it. This asymmetry is what makes the apparatus work. When all-knowing `S2` occupies the dominant place, the nature of truth becomes still more obscure. The truth of the modern system does not simply appear through accumulation of knowledge. Lacan connects this with the production of people themselves as consumable products or “human material,” thereby preparing his later analysis of surplus-jouissance and the social production of objects.

#### The psychoanalytic act and the hysterization of discourse

Lacan then shifts from social mastery to the analytic act. He distinguishes the analyst's discourse as a formal discourse from the discourse actually spoken by the analysand. Analytic experience is instituted through what he calls the hysterization of discourse. The analyst introduces, under artificial conditions, the structure of the hysteric's discourse.

This does not mean that hysteria is a personality description or that only women occupy it. Lacan explicitly notes that men who enter analysis are also required, by the rule of the analytic game, to pass through the hysteric's discourse. The point is structural. The speaking subject is brought into a position from which a question is addressed to a master signifier and from which knowledge is demanded and produced.

Lacan links this to the impossibility of a harmonious sexual relation at the level of signifiers. The existence of signifiers does not make human beings naturally understand one another. On the contrary, because relations are mediated by signifiers, misunderstanding is structural. What analytic practice does is not repair a lost natural harmony, but make the impasse speak.

#### The hysteric's desire to know and the production of the master

The hysteric, in Lacan's formulation, fabricates a man animated by a desire to know. He links this to a historical question he had raised previously: how did the master come to appropriate the slave's knowledge and turn it into the master's knowledge? The slave already satisfies the master's wants before the master knows them, so the master's acquisition of a desire to know cannot be treated as self-evident. Lacan provocatively suggests that the philosophical discourse itself may have played the hysteric's role in producing the master's desire to know.

The hysteric's discourse is therefore not reducible to a complaint. It produces a master who is compelled to generate knowledge. The divided subject `$` addresses `S1`, and the production is `S2`. But the truth beneath the speaking subject is `a`. This arrangement shows why the hysteric's question is tied to the value of the subject herself as object. What matters is not merely that a man know something in general, but that the Other be made to know what object she becomes within the discourse.

Lacan situates analytic free association inside this structure. The analysand is invited to say whatever comes, apparently abandoning ordinary reference. Yet the random production of signifiers is not structurally random. It bears on a knowledge that is not known but is at work in the signifying chain. The analyst's task cannot therefore be reduced to accumulating an encyclopedia of associations or applying a mechanical key to them.

#### Analyst's knowledge, object `a`, and Hegel

The analyst does have knowledge, but its place is not that of the dominant master. In the analyst's discourse, `S2` is placed beneath `a`, in the position of truth. The analyst's know-how may be acquired from analytic experience, but it does not occupy the manifest command position. The analyst is structurally placed as object `a`, and Lacan postpones the fuller explanation of why this must be so.

This leads him back to Hegel. He calls Hegel “the most sublime of hysterics” because the Hegelian historical machine pushes knowledge toward absolute knowledge while masking the loss and failure that animate the process. For Lacan, absolute knowledge would erase the dialectic between knowledge and jouissance that psychoanalysis has uncovered. Psychoanalysis instead keeps open the point where knowledge fails, where something is lost, and where truth is only partially available.

#### Enigma, citation, and interpretation

Lacan closes the chapter by asking what it means for `S2`, knowledge, to occupy the place of truth in the analyst's discourse. His answer is developed through two models of interpretation: enigma and citation.

An enigma gives an utterance whose statement has to be produced by the hearer. It is a half-saying: the utterance is present, but its completion is not. Lacan uses the riddle of the Sphinx and Oedipus to show that solving an enigma is not innocent. The answer has consequences, and Oedipus's successful answer is bound to the later trajectory that bears his name. The point is not that the analyst should present riddles, but that interpretation can function by offering an articulated fragment whose completion cannot be guaranteed by the interpreter.

Citation works differently. A citation inserts a statement under the authority of another name. The same words attributed to different authors do not have the same discursive effect. Citation therefore demonstrates that the sense of an utterance depends on the discourse in which it is inserted and on the place from which it is authorized. Lacan uses Marx and Freud as examples because invoking either name situates the reader within a pre-existing discursive field.

Interpretation can use both operations. It may extract an enigmatic fragment from the analysand's discourse or cite back to the analysand something already said, shifting its place and therefore its effect. This is tied to transference, but Lacan resists the simple idea that the analyst is merely the person who is “supposed to know.” The analysand is granted freedom to speak precisely so that a knowledge not consciously owned may be produced. The analyst, prepared in advance to become the product or remainder of the analytic operation, is destined to fall from the process rather than consolidate himself as master.

The chapter ends by restating the analyst's position as cause of the analysand's desire. Lacan notes that the function of such a cause is not historically unprecedented and hints at ancient predecessors, including Empedocles, but leaves this path for later development.

Session date: 17 December 1969.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter II, “The master and the hysteric,” printed pp. 29-38.

---

### III. Knowledge, a means of jouissance

Source location: Jacques Lacan, Seminar XVII, Chapter III, printed pp. 39-53. Session dated 14 January 1970.

#### Reintroducing the four discourses

Lacan again writes the four discourse formulas on the board. He emphasizes that they are generated from one another by circular permutation while the order of the four terms remains fixed. Their simplicity is deceptive: the fact that the same four terms produce structurally different discourses by changing place is the point of the formalization.

The title page again presents the complete set:

```text
U:  S2 -> a      M:  S1 -> S2      H:  $ -> S1      A:  a -> $
    S1    $          $     a           a    S2          S2   S1
```

The chapter's explicit themes are translation, the dominant positions of discourse, facts of structure, repetition and jouissance, entropy, and the impotence of truth.

#### The university translation and the condition of the unconscious

Lacan begins with a retrospective on how his teaching has been translated into academic discourse. He recalls the Bonneval conference on the unconscious and the work by Jean Laplanche and Serge Leclaire. He also comments on academic theses that attempt to systematize his work. The problem is not simply whether they are intelligent or well-intentioned. The university discourse exerts a structural pressure on what it receives, tending to translate a discourse with its own laws into the style and assumptions of established knowledge.

His key example is the reversal between two propositions: “language is the condition of the unconscious” and “the unconscious is the condition of language.” Lacan insists on the former. Academic translation can invert the direction and thereby give the claim a significance contrary to what he is saying. This is not merely an accidental mistake by a commentator. It illustrates how university discourse transforms what it incorporates.

Lacan includes himself in the problem. Teaching from a podium exposes even his own discourse to refraction by the university setting. The position of teacher carries prestige and tends toward institutional role-playing. He therefore treats the very existence and position of “a psychoanalyst” as something requiring structural explanation, not something to be settled by imitation, certification, ritual, or professional selection procedures.

#### The analyst as object `a` and the “dominant” place

Lacan states that the psychoanalyst's position is substantially made from object `a`. Object `a` is the discourse's reject-producing effect, the remainder that is at once opaque and essential. In the analyst's discourse it also occupies the place from which the discourse is ordered.

He temporarily calls the upper-left place the “dominant.” This does not mean that every discourse is simply a relation of domination in the everyday sense. The name indicates the term occupying the organizing place and helps distinguish the four structures. In the master's discourse, `S1` occupies it and can be approached through the law. In the hysteric's discourse, the dominant appears in the form of the symptom. In the analyst's discourse, the analyst has to represent the reject-effect, object `a`.

The difficulty is to characterize the dominant of the university discourse. Lacan treats this not as a settled definition but as an active research problem. This uncertainty is itself instructive: the formulas are supposed to show structural constraints, including impossibilities, rather than merely attach ready-made labels to social institutions.

#### Structure and impossibility

Lacan invites the audience to test the four positions combinatorially. If the terms must rotate while their order remains constrained, not every arbitrary arrangement is possible. The impossibility encountered by trying to permute the positions is not a defect of the model. It is the elementary mark of structure.

This formal point is decisive for psychoanalysis. Structure is not a decorative grid placed over clinical material after the fact. The encounter with impossibility is already present in analytic experience. The formalization isolates it rather than inventing it.

#### Freud, repetition, and the search for jouissance

The chapter then turns to Freud's second major step after the discovery of the unconscious. The unconscious made it possible to situate desire, but *Beyond the Pleasure Principle* forced Freud to introduce repetition. Lacan argues that what necessitates repetition is jouissance.

Repetition is not simply a biological cycle of need and satisfaction and not a return to equilibrium. Freud's death drive indicates that repetition touches something that goes against life. The pleasure principle itself functions as a principle of least tension, setting limits to jouissance. Repetition shows that these limits are crossed and that something returns beyond the regulation of pleasure.

Yet repetition does not restore the same thing intact. Each repetition involves loss. Lacan links this to Kierkegaard and makes the loss central: what repeats is marked by a reduction in jouissance. The Freudian lost object arises at this point. The repetitive circuit produces a defect, a failure, a lost quantity, and this loss becomes structurally decisive.

#### The unary trait and the origin of signifying knowledge

Lacan's specific contribution is to read the simplest mark, the unary trait, as the origin of the signifier in this field. Repetition is possible because a mark can be repeated. The signifier is not derived from a natural harmony between organism and environment. It begins with the mark and with the difference introduced by marking.

This is why Lacan rejects an appeal to “natural knowledge” that would supposedly orient the organism innately toward its world. He invokes scientific findings about perception to underline the fabricated and filtered character of the senses. Human vision and hearing do not transparently disclose a naturally matched world. The philosophical subject of knowledge, constructed from sensation, abstraction, and generalization, therefore cannot be equated with the subject of the signifier.

The subject of the signifier is an effect of one signifier representing a subject for another signifier. Lacan even draws on Aristotle's distinction of *hypokeimenon* from substance or essence to emphasize the “underneath” status of the subject: it is not a positive substance hidden behind the signifier.

#### Knowledge as an apparatus and the production of entropy

The link between `S1` and `S2` provides the elementary articulation of knowledge. Lacan connects the formal necessities of writing and modern logic with the operation of analytic repetition. The same formal logic that permits exact manipulation of symbols gives him a model for thinking knowledge as an apparatus rather than as conscious understanding.

At this point he introduces entropy. Repetition, by producing a loss of jouissance, generates something comparable to entropy. Lacan plays on the French sound of *entropie* and *anthropie*, but his point is not a physical reduction of psychoanalysis to thermodynamics. Energetics itself is described as a network of signifiers laid over the physical world. Once work, energy, conservation, and loss are formalized, the physical process becomes legible through a signifying apparatus.

The signifier is therefore an apparatus of jouissance. When the mark is introduced, an entropy becomes legible and something lost can be isolated. That lost term is what Lacan calls `a`. Object `a` is not first a concrete oral, anal, scopic, or vocal object and only later formalized. Those partial objects can come to occupy the function because `a` is first the structural loss produced by signifying articulation.

#### Mark, body, fantasy, and surplus-jouissance

Lacan illustrates the relation of mark and body through fantasy and practices such as flagellation. What matters is not exoticism but the fact that a mark can make the body itself into an object of jouissance. The body is not simply a biological substrate; the signifying mark reorganizes its relation to pleasure and loss.

This leads directly to surplus-jouissance. Jouissance is not simply a forbidden positive quantity waiting intact behind prohibition. It acquires status through loss. The loss introduced by repetition calls forth a surplus that appears as recoverable. Lacan had introduced *Mehrlust*, surplus-jouissance, on the model of Marx's surplus-value. Entropy gives him the dimension in which a lost quantity can become the basis for a surplus to be recovered.

Knowledge at work is therefore a means of jouissance. Its work produces loss, and that loss is the regular point at which access to the nature of jouissance becomes possible. This is why the chapter title is literal: knowledge does not merely describe jouissance from outside; in its signifying operation it participates in the production, loss, and recovery of jouissance.

#### Truth, half-saying, and the analyst's position

The final movement reconnects knowledge to truth. In the master's discourse, knowledge appears on the slave's side, but analytic experience forces a revision of the Hegelian picture according to which labor simply yields truth and ultimately absolute knowledge. Truth is accessible only through a half-saying. Beyond the half-said there is not a hidden totality waiting to be completed by more discourse.

Lacan reintroduces interpretation as an utterance that leaves the statement in reserve. This is why analytic interpretation cannot be equated with a fully explanatory proposition. The analyst's knowledge must function in the place of truth and therefore under the constraint of half-saying.

He then asks about the “love of truth.” Truth is marked by lack in being, by the impossibility of becoming full presence. The desire for truth can veil the very weakness it is attached to. Lacan recalls his formula that love gives what one does not have and associates the universal love of truth with a veil over castration.

The transferential situation does not therefore rest on the analyst really possessing complete knowledge. The analysand is invited to speak as though a knowledge could be produced, while the analyst himself must not occupy the place of a complete knower. What is expected from an analyst is that his knowledge function in terms of truth. This is why the analyst limits himself to half-saying.

Lacan closes by applying Freud's formula *Wo es war, soll Ich werden* to the analyst's position. The analyst does not occupy the dominant place for himself. He is called to come to the place where surplus-jouissance and the Other's jouissance were operative, as the support of the psychoanalytic act.

Session date: 14 January 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter III, “Knowledge, a means of jouissance,” printed pp. 39-53.

---

### IV. Truth, the sister of jouissance

Source location: Jacques Lacan, Seminar XVII, Chapter IV, printed pp. 54-68. Session dated 21 January 1970.

#### The reverse side and the problem of truth

Lacan opens by returning to the relation among the discourses. The analytic discourse completes the quarter-turn that generates the four structures, but this completion does not resolve the other three or provide a standpoint outside discourse from which they can finally be mastered. The “other side” does not explain the front in the manner of a hidden essence. The relation is one of weaving, texture, and reversal within language.

The title deliberately associates truth with jouissance. Lacan's task is to show that truth cannot be purified into a transparent proposition and detached from the effects of language, lack, desire, and jouissance.

The chapter title page displays three of the discourse formulas, university, hysteric, and master, while the opening prose says that analytic discourse completes the rotational system. The formulas therefore remain the formal background for the inquiry into truth.

#### Truth cannot be caught as a whole

Lacan distinguishes the logical use of truth as a value in propositional logic from the analytic problem of truth. In logic, truth can be reduced to a symbol or value. In psychoanalysis, the word provokes a different problem because truth cannot be handled as though it were a complete object.

He repeats his claim that truth is only ever half-said. Images of the “other side,” of the half-body, and of something hidden behind the visible surface illustrate the temptation to imagine that the missing half could simply be recovered. Lacan resists that temptation. The absence is not merely an accidentally hidden piece of information. Truth is structurally linked to a missing part.

Frege's notation of assertion gives him an entry into the relation between what is said and the claim that it is true. A proposition is composed of signifiers and bears sense, but the truth of the proposition cannot be reduced to the objects supposedly represented by those signifiers. Lacan uses examples of apparent nonsense, including Husserlian formulations, to show that sense and nonsense are not simple opposites. The *pas-de-sens* carries the ambiguity of “no sense” and “step of sense.” Witty formations demonstrate that a break in ordinary sense can carry a decisive effect.

The truth therefore escapes at the moment one tries to capture it as a full content. Lacan associates this with the dream: one wakes at the point where the dream might let truth drop, only to continue dreaming in reality. Truth appears in interruption, displacement, equivocation, and the failure of a smooth discourse.

#### Wittgenstein and the reduction of truth to grammatical structure

Lacan then turns to Wittgenstein's *Tractatus*. He treats it as the most forceful attempt to restrict truth to what can be articulated propositionally. On this reading, grammatical or logical structure constitutes the world; facts are what can be stated, and complex propositions are generated according to formal rules. The resulting system is tautological in the sense that what can be validly said is governed entirely by the formal possibilities of the system.

Lacan is fascinated by the rigor of this operation but treats its result as an extreme evacuation of truth. Everything that can be said is reduced to the logical game, while truth as such is pushed out of discourse. He provocatively describes the ferocity of this operation as psychotic. His point is not a clinical diagnosis based on biography, but the formal effect of a discourse that eliminates the speaker from what is said and refuses the place where truth would return as division.

He emphasizes that “it is day” becomes a fact only by being said. The proposition can be true, but the fact that it is true is not itself just another fact internal to the proposition. The uttering position cannot be cleanly absorbed into the statement. Lacan uses this to reject the fantasy of a final metalanguage. Attempts to stand as the Other of the discourse and certify it from outside reproduce the desire to occupy the position of the Other.

The logical paradoxes of implication similarly show that truth-value is not equivalent to ordinary sense. The notorious consequence that a false proposition can imply a true one reveals that formal truth functions according to rules that do not coincide with lived or semantic obviousness. Lacan uses this gap to reopen the analytic question of truth rather than to reject logic.

#### Truth, language, and university discourse

The analytic thesis is that truth is inseparable from the effects of language. There is no truth outside the field in which it is stated, and the true can emerge only against the possibility of the false. Lacan therefore again insists that language is the condition of the unconscious, not the reverse. To make the unconscious the condition of language would tend toward an absolute sense that analytic experience does not support.

The university discourse tries to stabilize knowledge in an apparently self-sufficient system. Yet beneath `S2`, in the place of truth, stands `S1`, the master signifier. Lacan interprets this as the persistence of the transcendental or commanding `I` beneath academic knowledge. Even systems that present themselves as impersonal knowledge cannot eliminate this hidden master-signifier function. The imperative reveals it particularly clearly.

His discussion of Georges Politzer extends the point. Politzer attacked academic psychology and recognized the importance of narrative and language in Freud's method, but Lacan argues that Politzer could not escape the demand for continuity of the `I`. The attempt to leave university discourse thereby re-enters it. The desire to preserve a coherent first person becomes the return of the master signifier beneath the critique.

#### “A child is being beaten” and the subject divided by jouissance

Lacan then tests the relation between proposition and truth through Freud's fantasy “A child is being beaten.” Grammatically it is a proposition, but the analytic question cannot be answered by labeling it simply true or false. The fantasy is sustained by a subject divided by jouissance.

The child who is beaten, the subject who states the fantasy, the father or other who strikes, and the jouissance attributed to the scene do not coincide in a single self-identical perspective. The fantasy organizes a relation in which the subject receives a message in inverted form and encounters his own jouissance through the imagined jouissance of the Other.

The figure of the father can remain unnamed and function as the support of jouissance. Lacan uses this to ask what can have a body without existing in the ordinary sense. His answer is the big Other. The Other can be treated as embodied in discourse even though it is not an empirical being.

#### Sade, materialism, and the sisterhood of truth and jouissance

The final movement turns to materialism and Sade. Lacan provocatively says that materialists are genuine believers insofar as matter is made into the final support. But the speaking being is not reducible to matter because language uses the speaking being and produces surplus-jouissance.

Sade's theoretical constructions are then read as an attempt to give jouissance an absolute support in Nature or God. The practitioner and the theoretician must be distinguished. The masochistic practitioner can organize a limited scene and obtain a local jouissance. Sade the theoretician goes further, imagining an unlimited natural or divine jouissance that would persist through destruction and repeated death.

Lacan links this to the “second death” discussed in connection with Antigone. Sade's theoretical wish for endless destruction is beyond practical reach. It becomes evidence of a love of truth: by refusing God and trying to abolish Him, the discourse simultaneously bears witness to the place it gives Him as support of jouissance.

This is where the title becomes precise. Truth is “sister” to jouissance because both arise from the effects of language and from a loss that cannot be made whole. Logical systems mark their limits through incompleteness; jouissance is likewise encountered through a limit, loss, and surplus. Truth is not identical with jouissance, but neither can it be separated from the structural operation that produces forbidden or lost jouissance.

Lacan closes with a play on the figure of the sister-in-law, referring to Minna Bernays and to Sade's own family situation. The anecdotal material does not replace the formal argument. It gives a final ironic turn to the chapter's insistence that the relation between truth and jouissance is neither pure abstraction nor transparent confession.

Session date: 21 January 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter IV, “Truth, the sister of jouissance,” printed pp. 54-68.

---

### V. The Lacanian field

Source location: Jacques Lacan, Seminar XVII, Chapter V, printed pp. 69-83 substantive text. Printed pp. 84-86 are non-substantive transition/divider matter before Chapter VI begins on p. 87. Session dated 11 February 1970.

#### Four discourses and the rejection of mastery

The chapter title page places the four discourse formulas in a two-by-two arrangement, again making clear that the Lacanian field is being developed through the rotations of the same four terms:

```text
MASTER (M)              UNIVERSITY (U)

   S1 -> S2                S2 -> a
   $     a                 S1    $

HYSTERIC (H)            ANALYST (A)

   $  -> S1                a  -> $
   a     S2                S2    S1
```

Lacan proposes a practical rule: a discourse can be classified by what it acknowledges it wants to master. The analyst's discourse must be situated at the opposite pole from any declared will to mastery. This is not because the analyst should merely dissimulate authority. The structure itself must be different from the discourse of mastery.

He contrasts this with the discourse of consciousness, whose synthetic ambition repeatedly returns. A consciousness that masters and unifies psychic life belongs to the very logic psychoanalysis has to displace. Lacan recalls his earlier dispute with Henri Ey and uses it to underline that analytic discourse cannot be reduced to a theory of a synthesizing conscious subject.

#### Freud, Marx, and discourse close to jouissance

Lacan says that Freud's discourse, like Marx's, has a special force because it does not evade the harsh point around which its discovery turns. Both are difficult to refute without replacing their structural insights with reassuring academic discourse.

Freud's distinctiveness lies in keeping his discourse close to jouissance. Yet Freud also masks or retreats from some of its consequences. Lacan gives feminine jouissance as an example and criticizes contemporary efforts to settle questions of orgasm by physiological observation or by appealing to the “total personality.” Such research, however technically sophisticated, misses the economic and discursive structure of jouissance that Freud's own discovery opened.

Lacan's aim is therefore not to add a biological theory of sexuality. He wants to expose the relation between discourse and jouissance more directly than Freud was able to do.

#### The jar of the Danaides and the happiness of the phallus

Jouissance is described through the image of the Danaides' leaking jars. Once the process is started, it does not arrive at a final filled state. A small excitation can escalate without a natural terminal measure. This is why jouissance cannot be defined as ordinary pleasure or successful biological satisfaction.

Lacan then attacks the post-Freudian ideal of the autonomous ego. The institutional celebration of ego autonomy represents, for him, a return to the master's discourse. Fifty years of psychoanalysis can thereby be presented as confirmation of adaptation, stability, and happiness, when the analytic discovery originally destabilized precisely these ideals.

He introduces the deliberately abrupt proposition that “the only happiness is the happiness of the phallus.” The point is not that the person possessing a penis is happy. On the contrary, the phallus functions as a privileged signifier whose jouissance is separated from the subject who bears it. The bearer cannot simply appropriate this jouissance as personal satisfaction.

Freud's hysterical examples, including the butcher's beautiful wife and Dora, show that desire is sustained by non-satisfaction. Satisfaction of demand does not settle desire. The desired object can be maintained elsewhere, transferred to another woman, or adored at a distance in such a way that lack is preserved. Lacan reads these structures as showing that phallic jouissance is excluded and substituted for by another economy organized around surplus-jouissance.

#### Sex, separation, and the non-biological status of the Freudian problem

Lacan explicitly warns against treating Freudian sexuality as a direct biological theory. He reflects on the word “sex,” distinguishing it from Greek terms connected with generation and nature and drawing attention to the Latin relation of *sexus* to cutting or separation.

The phallus is privileged not because it is the biological essence of sexuality but because its jouissance can be isolated and treated as excluded. Human sexual organization is therefore not explained by reproductive complementarity. Lacan contrasts it with animal examples in which sexual functions can be biologically integrated in quite different ways.

Desire belongs to another order. In the human tradition it is Eros as presentation of lack. The question is not simply what natural object is missing, but how lack is instituted through discourse.

Lacan returns to the mother as a privileged site in the organization of the child's dependence and jouissance. Woman appears within this discourse through masquerade and through the mediation of repetition. The social organization of sexual difference translates organic difference into a signifying structure in which the male organ is excluded as a direct bearer of complete jouissance and woman can be produced as object in relation to what the male renounces.

This section is not yet the later formal theory of sexuation, but it moves decisively away from a naturalist account. Sexual difference is being treated through discourse, prohibition, lack, and surplus-jouissance.

#### The political question and the hidden truth of mastery

Lacan then asks about psychoanalysis and politics. The relevant political intrusion is possible only if discourse is treated as a discourse of jouissance. The master's discourse has a hidden truth, but “hidden” does not mean a secret content waiting passively behind appearances. The truth is compressed in the structure and has to be unfolded.

Hegel's master-slave dialectic placed the truth of the master in the work of the slave and envisaged the historical production of absolute knowledge. Lacan argues that Marx has already undermined this prospect. Work does not simply generate knowledge. Knowledge is a means of jouissance, while work can produce truth and loss without yielding the Hegelian reconciliation.

The decisive historical transformation is the extraction and transfer of the slave's knowledge. What had belonged to the slave as know-how is appropriated and formalized in the master's system. The slave pays by losing his privileged relation to the means of jouissance, and the product `a` emerges as surplus-jouissance.

#### Thermodynamics, formalization, and the modern master

Lacan brings back thermodynamics to describe the modern organization of knowledge. The conservation of energy and the inevitable loss registered by the second law provide a formal analogy for a system in which what counts is precisely what can be written and counted.

He stresses that this is not Hegelian absolute knowledge. It is a different regime: a knowledge stripped down to formal calculation. In this regime, `S2` takes the dominant position of university discourse. The worker can be reduced to a unit of value, and surplus-jouissance becomes inscribed as surplus-value in an accounting system.

Marx denounces this process as spoliation, but Lacan shifts attention toward the knowledge that makes the process possible. Surplus-value is a social memorial or equivalent of surplus-jouissance. Consumer society becomes possible when persons and products are rendered homogeneous within a system of equivalent values and when industrial production manufactures imitations of surplus-jouissance.

#### The master, the wealthy, and the appropriation of knowledge

Lacan finally distinguishes the ancient master from the wealthy. The rich are not simply masters in the classical sense. Their power lies in purchase and accumulation. Reading political economy from Adam Smith onward, he provocatively says that wealth is the property of the wealthy and that the wealthy buy without truly paying for what matters most.

What they do not pay for is knowledge. In relations between developed and less-developed nations, a transaction presented as exchange can strip the other side of the knowledge that gave it status. The wealthy acquire that knowledge as well as commodities.

This returns the chapter to the analyst. The analyst's relation to knowledge cannot imitate the wealthy or the master by appropriating it. The function of the analyst has to be reconstructed from the place of object `a` and from failure, not mastery. Lacan closes by saying that everything hinges on failure and promises to explain the analyst's function from this point in the following session.

Session date: 11 February 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter V, “The Lacanian field,” printed pp. 69-83 substantive text; transition matter pp. 84-86 before Chapter VI.

## BEYOND THE OEDIPUS COMPLEX

### VI. The castrated master

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter VI, printed pp. 87-101. Session dated 18 February 1970.

#### Turning the discourse and locating the reverse side of psychoanalysis

Lacan opens by returning to the formal claim announced in the title of the seminar: the “other side” of psychoanalysis is not a psychological inversion but a structural turning of the discourse. The point is to identify the discourse whose reversal permits analytic discourse to emerge. He states directly that the master's discourse supplies the relevant matrix. Philosophy, in the tradition Lacan is interrogating, is already implicated in this master's discourse, and psychoanalysis can be situated only by showing how its own operation turns that discourse.

This is why the chapter begins with the relations among the four positions rather than with a new list of concepts. The terms do not acquire their meaning independently and then enter the formulas. Their function depends on where they are placed. Lacan repeatedly resists the temptation to treat `S1`, `S2`, `$`, and `a` as isolated substances. Their effect comes from the discourse that arranges them.

The four essential functions can be schematized, in the master's discourse, as follows:

```text
master signifier (S1)  ->  knowledge (S2)
---------------------      --------------
subject ($)                 jouissance / a
```

The upper-left term commands or initiates. The upper-right is the field toward which the discourse is directed and in which work is carried out. The lower-left is the truth that supports the dominant term without being directly avowed. The lower-right is what the operation produces and also what is lost. Lacan's argument throughout the chapter depends on keeping these places distinct from the terms that temporarily occupy them.

#### Knowledge, the body, and the signifier that makes the slave work

Lacan then asks where knowledge is situated. He returns to the relation between the body and the signifier, recalling the way the subject first confronts itself through an image and through the Other's signifiers. Knowledge is not a transparent interior possession. It is articulated through signifiers before the subject masters it.

The master's discourse makes this especially visible. `S1`, the master signifier, addresses `S2`, knowledge. The effect is not that the master becomes knowledgeable. The master commands and sets knowledge to work. The slave, in the classical figure, is the one who knows how to do things. The slave possesses a practical knowledge of production, craft, and the master's requirements. The master does not need to know the work. What matters structurally is that the master signifier imposes an order under which knowledge functions.

Lacan uses Hegel's master-slave relation here, but he does not simply repeat it. The point is to isolate what the discourse structure lets one see. The master's ignorance is not an accidental defect to be repaired by education. It is constitutive of the master's place. The master's command functions precisely because the work of knowledge is displaced onto the Other.

The result is the production of a remainder, `a`, linked to surplus-jouissance. What is produced cannot be reintegrated into a complete system of satisfaction. The master's discourse therefore carries loss within its own operation. The master's apparent sovereignty conceals the divided subject `$` in the place of truth and generates a remainder of jouissance in the place of production.

#### From the master to the hysteric

Lacan next contrasts the master's discourse with the hysteric's discourse. The hysteric places the divided subject in the dominant position and addresses a master signifier. This is not a personality portrait. It is a way of formalizing the demand that a master produce knowledge about the subject's division.

```text
HYSTERIC

   $   ->  S1
   --      --
   a       S2
```

The hysteric's discourse is therefore structurally productive. It makes the master work. Lacan emphasizes that the hysteric wants a master, but not one who can simply enjoy undisturbed. The master must know, must answer, must produce `S2`. The hysteric provokes the master into knowledge while maintaining the gap that prevents any answer from closing the question of desire.

This lets Lacan return to the clinical material of hysteria, especially Dora. What matters in Dora's relation to her father is not a simple family drama to be reduced to biographical characters. The father occupies the position of a master who is already marked by insufficiency. His impotence is not merely a defect to be corrected. It is the condition under which the hysteric's question can be sustained.

Dora supports the father's desire while at the same time interrogating what a woman is for the Other. The figures around her, including Frau K. and Herr K., enter into this circuit. Lacan's reconstruction is concerned with how the hysteric's desire is organized around knowledge, lack, and the Other's desire. The hysteric's relation to the father is therefore not simply one of obedience or rebellion. She makes the father into a castrated master, a master from whom knowledge is demanded precisely because mastery is incomplete.

#### The hysteric's question and the master's failure

Lacan sharpens the point by saying that the hysteric wants a master she can reign over. The formulation is deliberately paradoxical. If the master could provide a complete answer, the hysteric's discourse would stop. But the structure depends on preserving the inadequacy of the answer. The master must keep producing knowledge without arriving at a final knowledge of the subject's desire.

This is why the hysteric's discourse reveals something hidden in the master's discourse. The latter masks the division of the subject. The hysteric places that division in the open. Through the hysteric's demand, the master's relation to knowledge becomes visible as fundamentally unstable.

The analyst cannot simply take over the master's place and supply the answer. If analysis did this, it would restore the master's discourse. Analytic discourse is instead produced by another turn, one in which the object `a` takes the dominant position and knowledge is displaced into the place of truth.

```text
ANALYST

   a   ->  $
   --      --
   S2      S1
```

Lacan stresses that the analyst's position is not that of the subject who knows everything. The analyst causes speech and knowledge to be produced from a different place. This is why the passage from hysteria to analytic discourse cannot be reduced to replacing one authority with a better-informed authority.

#### Jouissance, prohibition, and the barrier in the master's discourse

The chapter then clarifies the role of jouissance. In the master's discourse there is a structural barrier at the lower level between the divided subject and the remainder `a`. The master cannot directly appropriate the surplus-jouissance produced by the operation. Lacan links this to prohibition. Jouissance is not simply absent; it is structurally interdicted.

This permits him to restate the relation between law and jouissance. Prohibition is not an external moral rule imposed on an otherwise naturally complete enjoyment. The discourse itself organizes the impossibility. The subject's division and the production of `a` are already effects of the signifying operation.

The relation can be indicated by the master's formula:

```text
MASTER

   S1  ->  S2
   --      --
   $       a
```

Lacan notes that fantasy, in its usual form `$ <> a`, cannot simply be written across the lower level of the master's discourse. The structure blocks such a direct relation. This is one reason why the master is blind to the fantasy that sustains him. Fantasy becomes legible elsewhere, particularly in analytic discourse, where the relation to object `a` can be articulated differently.

#### Freud, Oedipus, and the production of the castrated father

From this point Lacan turns explicitly to Freud's Oedipus complex. He does not reject the Oedipal material, but he refuses to leave it at the level of family narrative. The crucial question is what structural function the myth performs.

Freud's Oedipal construction makes the father central to prohibition, desire, and access to the mother. Yet Lacan argues that the psychoanalytic father is already a father marked by castration. The father who functions in the structure is not the omnipotent possessor of all enjoyment. The clinical father is repeatedly encountered as limited, lacking, compromised, or unable fully to embody the law he represents.

This gives the chapter its title. The master who interests psychoanalysis is a castrated master. The father's authority is not founded on actual plenitude. The hysteric in particular reveals this by putting the father's insufficiency to work. She demands knowledge from a father whose limitation sustains her question.

Lacan's criticism is directed against taking Freud's Oedipal mythology literally. If the father were simply the empirical agent who possesses the mother and imposes prohibition, one would miss the structural contradiction. The father operates through the signifier and through a function that exceeds the particular person.

#### Castration as structural rather than anatomical

The chapter closes by bringing the discussion of castration back to the discourse structure. Castration cannot be reduced to bodily mutilation, threat, or anatomical absence. It designates the effect by which jouissance is limited and desire is produced through the signifier.

This is why the father's own castration matters. The father can function as a signifier of law only because he does not coincide with complete jouissance. The image of an all-powerful father would abolish the very lack through which desire is articulated.

Lacan therefore prepares the next chapters by shifting the question from “Who is the father?” to the relation among father, law, knowledge, truth, and jouissance. The Oedipus complex will be examined not as a complete explanatory story but as one mythic articulation of a structure that must be isolated more rigorously.

Session date: 18 February 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter VI, “The castrated master,” printed pp. 87-101.

### VII. Oedipus and Moses and the father of the horde

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter VII, printed pp. 102-117. Session dated 11 March 1970.

#### Truth as a place and the masking of the subject

Lacan begins by stating that analytic discourse draws its importance from the fact that the truth of the master's discourse is masked. To speak of a “place of truth” is not to claim that a proposition becomes true merely by occupying a box in the discourse formula. The structural place indicates where the support of the dominant term lies and why it cannot fully appear in the discourse that depends on it.

He now gives greater functional precision to the positions. The upper-left is the place of command or dominant agency. The lower-left is truth. What is placed in the position of truth does not command directly. It supports the dominant term while remaining only partially articulated.

Lacan also restates the equivalence of positions across discourses. The upper-left place occupied by `S1` in the master's discourse is the same structural place occupied by `S2` in the university discourse:

```text
M (S1)  ~=  U (S2)
```

The point is not that `S1` and `S2` mean the same thing. It is that both can occupy the same dominant position in different discourses. This distinction between place and term is essential to the quarter-turn logic.

The master's discourse masks the division of the subject because `$` is placed beneath `S1` as its truth. Lacan returns to the formula “Either I am not thinking or I am not,” using it to show that the subject of the unconscious cannot be gathered into an indivisible identity. Where the subject seems most certain of itself, the signifying structure produces a split.

Truth itself therefore appears only as half-saying. Lacan recalls the enigma and the question “What is truth?” to underline that truth cannot be totalized into complete knowledge. What can be said of truth is structurally limited.

#### The master's discourse, fantasy, and the prohibition of jouissance

Lacan then reintroduces the master formula and stresses the barrier at the lower level:

```text
   S1  ->  S2
   --      --
   $   [barrier]  a
```

Surplus-jouissance is produced in the master's discourse, but the master has no direct relation to the truth that supports him or to the remainder produced by the work of knowledge. Jouissance is therefore prohibited at the structural level rather than merely forbidden by a moral command.

This also explains why fantasy does not fit neatly into the master's discourse. The fantasy relation `$ <> a` cannot simply be inscribed across the lower level because the barrier prevents the relation from functioning there as a direct circuit. Lacan interprets this as one basis of the master's blindness.

The analyst's discourse changes the situation because knowledge `S2` is placed in the position of truth. Analytic knowledge therefore does not appear as publicly displayed mastery. It functions beneath the analyst's position as object `a`, causing the divided subject to speak and master signifiers to be produced.

Lacan uses this distinction to criticize the modern demand that all knowledge be made explicit, complete, and scientifically available. Psychoanalytic knowledge does not become truth by being expanded into a total body of doctrine. Its structural place is different.

#### Myth as the field of half-saying

The discussion then moves to myth. Lacan notes that modern linguistics, especially Lévi-Strauss, has shown that myths are structured through relations and transformations rather than by a single literal narrative. He uses this to connect myth with half-saying. Myth does not simply conceal one final proposition waiting to be translated into plain language. Its contradictions and variants are part of the way truth is articulated.

This allows him to question the privileged status psychoanalysis has given to the Oedipus myth. The mythographers themselves are not impressed by psychoanalysis's tendency to elevate Oedipus into a universal key. Lacan cites Lévi-Strauss's structural treatment of myth to insist that one must examine the relations among variants and oppositions rather than treat one narrative as self-sufficient.

At the same time, Lacan does not dismiss Freud's myths as mere mistakes. Their very distortion is significant. Freud's *Totem and Taboo*, *Moses and Monotheism*, and the Oedipus complex are treated as formations whose contradictions point toward a structural problem Freud was trying to articulate.

#### Totem and Taboo: the father of the horde

Lacan returns to the father of the primal horde. In Freud's story, the old father monopolizes the women and is killed by the sons. The killing does not liberate unrestricted enjoyment. Instead, it produces fraternity, guilt, prohibition, and law.

Lacan emphasizes the strangeness of this construction. If the goal were simply to explain access to the women, killing the father should open enjoyment. Freud's myth produces the opposite result: the dead father becomes more powerful as law. The prohibition is strengthened after the murder.

This is one reason Lacan refuses to reduce the story to anthropology. The empirical plausibility of a prehistoric horde is not the decisive issue. What matters is the structure Freud creates: the dead father and jouissance become linked. The father's death does not abolish law but inaugurates it.

Lacan also draws out the political implication of Freud's fraternity. The brothers become brothers through the murder and the pact that follows. He provocatively associates fraternity with segregation. Human brotherhood is not a natural starting point. It is formed through exclusion, boundary, and common prohibition. He therefore treats appeals to universal brotherhood with suspicion, since the creation of an inside can imply the production of an outside.

#### Moses and the return of the murdered father

Lacan next turns to *Moses and Monotheism*. Here again Freud's construction depends on murder. Moses must be killed, after which the event returns through repression, memory, tradition, and the prophets.

Lacan is struck by the insistence with which Freud requires the murder. The question is not simply whether the historical reconstruction is correct. Freud needs the dead father structurally. The murder permits the father to return in a form stronger than the living person.

This motivates Lacan's interest in Ernst Sellin, whose biblical exegesis Freud used to support the hypothesis that Moses was murdered. Lacan notes that he has been trying to obtain Sellin's book and has already begun reading Hosea independently. This preparation leads directly to Chapter IX.

The Moses material also exposes a difference between Oedipus and the father-of-the-horde myth. In Sophocles, Oedipus does not know that he has killed his father or married his mother. The tragedy turns on truth, recognition, and the consequences of having answered the Sphinx. In *Totem and Taboo*, by contrast, the brothers knowingly kill the father and then institute prohibition. The two stories cannot simply be placed in the same basket.

#### Oedipus as Freud's dream

Lacan therefore argues that Freud's use of Oedipus has to be analyzed rather than accepted as a transparent foundation. In Sophocles, murder of the father and jouissance of the mother are linked to an ordeal of truth. Oedipus gains access to Jocasta after triumphing in a test of knowledge, the Sphinx's riddle. He is not simply the beneficiary of a murder; he is caught in a structure in which truth returns against him.

The Freud of psychoanalysis, however, extracts from this tragedy a general mythic schema. Lacan suggests that the Oedipus complex should itself be treated as Freud's dream. This does not mean it is useless. It means that its manifest form must be interpreted.

The chapter ends by distinguishing three different mythic constructions that Freud had brought together: Oedipus, the father of the primal horde, and Moses. Each articulates murder, fatherhood, truth, law, and jouissance differently. The task is to move from these narratives to the structural relation they imperfectly express.

Session date: 11 March 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter VII, “Oedipus and Moses and the father of the horde,” printed pp. 102-117.

### VIII. From myth to structure

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter VIII, printed pp. 118-132, including the supplement “The following session: Radiophonie.” Main session dated 18 March 1970; supplement dated 8 April 1970.

#### The dead father does not liberate jouissance

Lacan opens by taking up the death of the father as the supposed key to psychoanalysis. He rejects the simple formula that the death of God or father would release desire from law. Freud's own construction points in the opposite direction. The dead father strengthens prohibition.

The relation between death of the father and jouissance therefore has to be reformulated. In the Oedipus story, the father's murder appears to be the condition for access to the mother, but Oedipus obtains this access only at the price of the murder and without knowing what he has done. The tragedy shows that the issue cannot be reduced to removal of an obstacle.

Lacan rereads the Sphinx episode as a trial of truth. Oedipus answers the enigma and thereby suppresses the suspense introduced by the question. The successful answer does not save him from truth; it helps place him on the path by which truth will return. Later, his eyes become a particularly vivid image of object loss. The point is not simply that he becomes blind. Lacan emphasizes the object-like status of the eyes that fall from him, a way of linking the tragic conclusion to castration and object `a` rather than to moral punishment.

The Oedipus myth thus does not merely teach that one must not desire the mother. It shows an entanglement of truth, desire, castration, and the object that cannot be captured by a prohibition alone.

#### Freud's dream of the father and the real as impossible

Lacan then turns to the dream of the dead father discussed by Freud, especially the phrase “He didn't know he was dead.” The formula interests Lacan because unconscious thought can be articulated around death while death itself remains unknowable from the standpoint of the living subject.

This gives a new angle on the dead father. The Freudian father of the myth is not merely a remembered person. He becomes a structural operator. In *Totem and Taboo*, the dead father and jouissance are made equivalent. The father who guards jouissance is precisely the father who is no longer present as a living empirical individual.

Lacan identifies this with the real insofar as the real is the impossible. The real father, in this structural sense, is not a psychological character who once exercised total power. He marks the impossible around which prohibition and jouissance are organized.

This is a decisive movement from myth to structure. The myth says that a primal father actually existed and was killed. The structure extracts the logical function: the impossible father is the operator that locates prohibition and jouissance.

#### Castration as operation of the signifier

The discussion of the father now becomes inseparable from castration. Lacan insists that castration is not merely a fantasy. It is a symbolic operation introduced by the incidence of the signifier into the sexual relation.

He recalls the classical distinctions among castration, frustration, and privation in order to make this point. Castration is symbolic. Frustration operates differently, and privation concerns a real lack. The father as agent of castration therefore cannot be reduced to the father as an empirical person who threatens punishment.

What matters is the structural place from which the operation is produced. A signifier can intervene in the sexual relation and produce a lack that reorganizes desire. The subject's relation to the phallus is therefore not adequately described by anatomy.

The real father is named as agent of castration, but Lacan immediately complicates this formulation. If the real father is the impossible, how can he be an agent? The word “agent” allows Lacan to suspend the assumption that agency means conscious personal causation. The agent can function as an instrument or bearer of an operation whose logic exceeds the individual.

#### Act, agent, and the master's agency

Lacan develops this distinction through the language of action and agency. An act, in psychoanalysis, is not simply a voluntary deed originating in an autonomous subject. It presupposes a field already structured by the signifier. The murder of the father in Freud's myth can therefore be treated as a statement about the impossible rather than as an anthropological report.

The “real father” and the “agent of castration” have to be located at this level. The father carries out the work of the master's agency insofar as the signifying structure assigns him that function.

Lacan then plays on the contemporary figure of the agent, including the double agent. The modern world is full of agents who mediate, represent, sell, arrange, and manipulate systems whose total structure they do not control. This becomes an analogy for the distinction between empirical person and structural function. The agent can carry an operation whose truth lies elsewhere.

He briefly moves through political examples, including the “Father of the People,” to show how fantasies of paternal mastery are lodged in discourse. The empirical father, by contrast, may simply be an ordinary man who works, feeds his family, and wants to be loved. The tyrannical omnipotent father belongs to another register.

#### The real father as effect of language

Lacan therefore states that the real father is a construction of language. He has no other real in the sense relevant to psychoanalysis. This does not mean that biological paternity is unreal. Lacan provocatively says that if one wanted the scientifically real father, one would arrive at the spermatozoon. But that biological fact has very little to do with the paternal function psychoanalysis is trying to articulate.

The analytic question concerns how a father functions within the symbolic organization of desire. Lacan even raises, provocatively, the possibility that the analyst can occupy the position of real father in an analysis without being the biological progenitor. The point is structural, not genealogical.

The question of the father's function also appears in relation to the mother's desire. Lacan repeats his famous image of the mother as a crocodile whose jaws may close on the child. The phallus operates like a roller or wedge that prevents the jaws from closing. The paternal metaphor is thus less the rule of a sovereign man than an operation that limits the mother's desire and introduces separation.

He stresses that this is where Freud's Oedipal account has to be reworked. The issue is not whether the actual father is strong enough. The real operation depends on a signifier and on the structural relation among desire, law, and castration.

#### The hysteric wants a master, but one who does not govern

From the father's function Lacan returns to the hysteric. The question “What does a woman want?” is not treated as a timeless statement about women. Lacan explicitly notes that the hysteric's structural position is not necessarily tied to one sex.

The hysteric's discourse produces the master signifier. She wants a master, but a specific kind of master: one who will be made to know, one she can question, and one whose mastery will remain incomplete. Lacan puts it sharply: she wants a master she can reign over. She wants him to produce knowledge, but not so much knowledge that her own place as the object or cause of his desire disappears.

This brings the chapter back to the obstacle of jouissance. In the analyst's discourse, Lacan again shows the structure in which object `a` addresses the divided subject while knowledge occupies the position of truth and `S1` is produced:

```text
ANALYST

   a   ->  $
   --      --
   S2      S1
```

The barrier of jouissance remains operative. Castration is articulated through this impossibility. Even the child, Lacan concludes, encounters a father who knows nothing about the truth of the function he occupies.

#### Supplement: “The following session: Radiophonie”

After the 18 March session, the text includes a supplement from 8 April 1970. Lacan explains that instead of improvising answers to several written questions, he will reply from prepared texts. The replies were later published as “Radiophonie.”

He notes that one of the questions concerns a statement in his *Écrits* that Freud anticipated, without knowing it, research associated with Saussure and the Prague Circle. This provides another example of the seminar's distinction between knowledge consciously possessed and a structure that can operate in a discourse before it is explicitly theorized.

Lacan also reflects on the conditions of speaking, writing, and interpretation. He distinguishes the written from the spoken and emphasizes that analytic interpretation cannot be treated as the simple delivery of a hidden message whose sense was already complete. The written questions will be answered in writing because the form of the response matters to what can be articulated.

He introduces the notion of a common language or *koine* in relation to the gap between constructed articulation and what common consciousness expects. The abrupt discourse of psychoanalysis can precipitate effects within ordinary language precisely because it does not merely reproduce the expectations already contained there.

The supplement closes with the announcement that the prepared replies will be given rather than improvised. The date is 8 April 1970.

Main session date: 18 March 1970. Supplement date: 8 April 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter VIII, “From myth to structure,” printed pp. 118-132, including the supplement “The following session: Radiophonie.”

### IX. Yahweh's ferocious ignorance

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter IX, printed pp. 133-140. Session dated 15 April 1970. Printed pp. 141-142 are transition/divider matter before Chapter X.

#### Introducing André Caquot and the problem of Sellin

Lacan begins by introducing André Caquot, Director of Studies in the Fifth Section of Sciences of Religion at the École Pratique des Hautes Études. The exchange is explicitly dialogical. Caquot's interventions must therefore be kept separate from Lacan's statements.

The immediate topic is Ernst Sellin's work and Freud's use of it in *Moses and Monotheism*. Lacan has been trying to understand the textual basis for Freud's insistence that Moses was murdered. He credits Caquot with helping him place Sellin within the history of biblical exegesis and with clarifying the scholarly setting in which Sellin's reconstruction was produced.

Lacan stresses his own ignorance. He distinguishes being knowledgeable in a field from what he calls putting oneself “on the scent” of a question. The title of the chapter is already active here. Ignorance is not simply lack of information. Lacan is interested in a form of not-knowing that can open a line of inquiry.

He links this to analysis. The analyst cannot be defined as the one who knows what everyone else does not. Psychoanalytic discourse depends on a different relation to knowledge, one that accepts that the analyst does not control the truth of what is said.

#### Biblical exegesis, false interpretation, and the written trace
