The Sellin question lets Lacan explore interpretation itself. Sellin reconstructed biblical texts in order to recover an event, the alleged murder of Moses, that was not plainly stated in the received text. Lacan is struck by the peculiar status of such reconstruction. If a hidden event can be recovered only by rearranging and redeciphering written traces, what kind of memory is being claimed?

He notes the ambiguity. Freud can use Sellin's hypothesis because it supports the idea that a memory persists despite resistance and conscious intention. Yet the persistence is located in writings. The text has to be reread and reconstructed before the hidden event emerges.

Caquot supplies important scholarly corrections. He explains changes between editions of Sellin and raises the possibility that Freud relied on a hypothesis whose status in Sellin's own later work was less secure than Freud's use might suggest. Lacan accepts the correction but insists that Freud does not build the whole of his theory on this textual detail. Sellin functions as support for something Freud already required structurally.

This exchange exemplifies the chapter's concern with false interpretation. An interpretation can be erudite, rigorous, and wrong. The issue is not merely accuracy of scholarship but the relation between a reconstruction and the desire that organizes it.

#### Hosea, invective, and Yahweh's relation to his people

Lacan then asks Caquot to help with Hosea. He has been struck by the ferocity of Yahweh's address to his people. The text is saturated with accusation, prostitution, betrayal, jealousy, and the language of marital relations.

Lacan is especially interested in the emergence of Yahweh as spouse. He suggests that Hosea marks a decisive moment in which the relation between God and people is articulated through a marital allegory. The language later familiar in the Christian image of Christ and the Church as bridegroom and bride has, in Lacan's reading, an antecedent here.

The discussion turns to Hebrew terms for man, woman, husband, and wife. Caquot clarifies the lexical relations. Lacan's interest is not philology for its own sake. He wants to see how a signifier can shift from naming sexual difference to naming a social or covenantal relation.

The exchange also touches on the relation between Yahweh and Baal. Caquot explains distinctions in usage that prevent a simple equation of the terms. Lacan's questions repeatedly expose the risk of reading a later theological system back into the biblical text.

#### Ignorance, fatherhood, and truth

Lacan returns to the word ignorance. To be a father, he says, is not simply to be the real father of an empirical child. The real father, as developed in the previous chapter, is structurally linked to the agent of castration. What the father must “ferociously ignore” is precisely the total knowledge that would collapse the symbolic function into omniscience.

This gives the title “Yahweh's ferocious ignorance” its force. Yahweh is not treated as a theological concept of an all-knowing being. Lacan is interested in the biblical God as a speaking figure who commands, accuses, desires, becomes jealous, and addresses a people in a discourse that does not present itself as transparent knowledge.

Truth, once again, is not total knowledge. One “falls upon” truth rather than mastering it. Lacan uses his own encounter with Caquot as an example of entering a field in which he is not expert and allowing the structure of the questions to organize inquiry.

The relation to analysis is direct. The analyst's position cannot be secured by pretending to possess complete biblical, historical, linguistic, or clinical knowledge. The relevant knowledge is one that functions within a discourse and can be displaced by interpretation.

#### Caquot's corrections and Freud's reading

The exchange becomes increasingly precise about Sellin. Lacan asks whether Freud read Sellin closely. Caquot replies that Freud did; the book is clear and rigorous, even if Caquot considers the hypothesis false. He explains that Sellin retained parts of the exegesis while later modifying or abandoning the claim that had been used to support Moses's death.

Lacan is less concerned with settling the historical verdict than with the structural use Freud makes of the hypothesis. Freud's theory needs the murder because the murdered father returns as law, memory, and truth. The scholarly uncertainty therefore does not dissolve the psychoanalytic problem. It makes clearer that the problem cannot be solved by historical confirmation alone.

This reinforces Lacan's distinction between mythic narration and structural function. The historical question “Was Moses murdered?” and the psychoanalytic question “Why does Freud need Moses to be murdered?” are not identical.

#### Hosea and the marital allegory

Lacan returns to Hosea's rhetoric. Yahweh accuses the people of prostitution and at the same time assumes the position of spouse. The apparent contradiction is precisely what interests him. The discourse combines condemnation and attachment, accusation and covenant.

Caquot explains the Hebrew usage and the relation between terms that can mean man, husband, woman, wife, and master. Lacan listens for the point at which the signifier produces a relation that is not reducible to biological sexuality.

The discussion therefore anticipates the seminar's larger claim that there is no natural sexual relation simply waiting to be expressed in language. The biblical text organizes relations through signifiers whose meanings are historical, juridical, religious, and erotic at once.

The chapter closes without converting the exchange into a final doctrine. Lacan explicitly values Caquot's expertise and lets the philological corrections stand. What matters for the seminar is that the dialogue has clarified how interpretation, textual reconstruction, knowledge, ignorance, truth, and the paternal function intersect.

Session date: 15 April 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter IX, “Yahweh's ferocious ignorance,” printed pp. 133-140; printed pp. 141-142 are transition/divider matter before Chapter X.

## THE OTHER SIDE OF CONTEMPORARY LIFE

### X. Interview on the steps of the Pantheon

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter X, printed pp. 143-149. Session dated 13 May 1970.

#### An interrupted seminar turned into an interview

This chapter is not presented as an ordinary seminar session. The Law Faculty in rue Saint-Jacques was closed, and Lacan met with a smaller group of students on the steps of the Pantheon. The recording therefore preserves a question-and-answer format. The anonymous student interventions, marked `X` in the edition, must be kept separate from Lacan's replies.

Lacan begins by saying that he had intended to give a recapitulation of the diachronic development that had brought the seminar to the present point, especially the elaboration of the master's discourse. The altered circumstances make him switch formats. Instead of reproducing the prepared exposition, he invites questions and uses them to clarify the relation among master discourse, psychoanalysis, philosophy, science, anxiety, the university, and the student situation.

The chapter consequently functions as a hinge. It looks backward to the formal construction of the four discourses and forward to the analysis of contemporary university and scientific discourse in the next chapters.

#### Affect, repression, and anxiety

One student raises the relation between existentialism and structuralism, another asks about Hegel, and the discussion quickly moves to the question of affect. Lacan responds to the criticism that his structural orientation neglects affect. He insists that this criticism misses what he had already done in Seminar X, where anxiety was treated as the central affect around which the clinical field was organized.

His point is not that affects are unreal or irrelevant. The Freudian distinction he wants to retain is that affect is not what is repressed. What undergoes repression is articulated through the representative of representation, while affect is displaced, detached from its original anchoring, and may become unrecognizable. This displacement is not an argument for ignoring affect; it is the very reason affect cannot simply be read as a transparent expression of an inner state.

The question of Kierkegaard gives Lacan an opportunity to distinguish psychoanalytic discourse from a philosophical genealogy of anxiety. He acknowledges that the concept of anxiety has a philosophical history and that Kierkegaard occupies an important place in it. What he resists is the idea that psychoanalysis is simply another philosophical position in the same lineage. The analytic articulation comes from a specific practice and from the structure that practice reveals.

Lacan also reiterates the formula from his earlier work that anxiety is not without an object. At the time of Seminar X, he had not yet named the object as surplus-jouissance in the vocabulary now available to him. The present seminar lets him retrospectively situate `object a` and surplus-jouissance within the discourse structures. This does not turn `a` into an ordinary empirical object. It remains the remainder around which anxiety is organized and which cannot be reduced to a nameable thing.

#### Psychoanalysis, philosophy, and the source of Lacan's claims

A student asks whether psychoanalytic practice gives Lacan ideas unavailable elsewhere. Lacan refuses the implication that he possesses a privileged stock of philosophical propositions. His sustained work over many years has been driven by the analytic experience, not by a desire to install himself in a philosophical canon.

He says that, without the experience of psychoanalysis, he would neither have the right nor the desire to extend philosophical discourse in the way he has done. The difficulty is that analytic discourse necessarily appears philosophically problematic because it is not organized around the same dominant position as philosophical mastery. Lacan therefore resists being placed comfortably alongside Kierkegaard, Ockham, Gorgias, or other figures merely because his work can be compared with them.

A student says that Lacan's discourse is constantly decentered in relation to sense. Lacan accepts the displacement but insists that it is not a stylistic game. Analytic discourse is structurally different. Its movement follows from the positions occupied by `a`, `$`, `S1`, and `S2`, not from a taste for paradox or obscurity.

#### The Other, incoherence, and science

Another question concerns the Other as the treasure trove of signifiers. The student asks whether the Other may contain incoherent elements and whether Lacan had claimed that it cannot be confronted. Lacan rejects the attribution and returns to the distinction between analytic discourse and the discourse of science.

He has recently read a critical discussion by Cornelius Castoriadis, who points to the continual displacement in Lacan's discourse and to its relation to science. Lacan accepts that his discourse has a precise reference to science, but not that it is simply scientific discourse. Analytic discourse is conditioned by the discourse of science. Science, as Lacan formulates it here, leaves no place for “man” as a humanist center. Psychoanalysis emerges in a historical field transformed by this scientific evacuation of the traditional subject.

This is why Lacan's relation to science is double. Psychoanalysis cannot simply be assimilated to science, yet it is not intelligible without the reorganization of knowledge produced by modern science. The next chapter will pursue this by introducing the alethosphere and the proliferation of objects produced by scientific discourse.

#### University discourse and the place of the exploited

The student discussion turns toward the university. Lacan asks what occupies the place of the exploited in university discourse. He answers: `a`. In the university structure, knowledge `S2` occupies the dominant position and addresses `a`. The divided subject `$` is produced.

The point is not that every student is psychologically an object. It is that the university discourse formalizes a social bond in which institutionalized knowledge operates as agent and acts on a term placed in the position of object. This is why Lacan can connect the formal schema to the unrest occurring around universities without reducing the unrest to individual motives.

He distinguishes the radicality emerging in contemporary events from the institutional function of the university itself. The university is linked to the state and to the circulation of the master's discourse. It is not simply the opposite of mastery. Rather, university discourse is one historical transformation of mastery, one in which knowledge comes to occupy the dominant place.

The masking of this function can fail. Lacan suggests that the university's relation to the master's discourse is becoming increasingly visible. What had operated under the appearance of neutral knowledge appears as a structured relation between knowledge, work, production, and the divided subject.

#### The proletarian, knowledge, and dispossession

A student asks about the proletarian. Lacan situates the question in relation to the master's discourse rather than answering with a sociological definition. The slave of the classical master's discourse possessed a know-how. Modern transformations of mastery alter this relation. The modern worker can be deprived not only of control over production but also of the knowledge that had once been bound to the work itself.

Lacan's emphasis is on the expropriation of knowledge. Modern production can remove practical know-how from the worker, relocate it in systems, management, science, and institutions, and return to the worker only a wage and a function. This changes the structural place of knowledge in the social bond.

The student question therefore leads to a sharper problem: can material labor, once separated from the knowledge that organized it, still by itself be the decisive subversive force? Lacan does not provide a political program. He reformulates the problem structurally. The issue is how knowledge is distributed, who is made to work, what is produced, and how the master's discourse changes when knowledge itself is reorganized.

The interview ends here, with the university and proletarian questions left open for the more systematic examination that follows.

Session date: 13 May 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter X, “Interview on the steps of the Pantheon,” printed pp. 143-149.

### XI. Furrows in the alethosphere

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter XI, printed pp. 150-163. Session dated 20 May 1970.

#### From the steps of the Pantheon back to discourse

Lacan opens by referring to the recent meeting on the Pantheon steps and to the exchange that took place there. The questions of students, science, knowledge, and the university now become the entry point for a more formal inquiry into the relation between language, number, repetition, science, and the production of objects.

He insists again that discourse is not simply a sequence of statements. A discourse is a structure that fixes places and determines relations. Its effects continue beyond the intentions of the individuals who speak within it. The move into mathematics in this chapter is therefore not an excursion away from psychoanalysis. It is an attempt to isolate the effects of repetition and the One without reducing them to psychology.

#### The unary trait, the One, and the divided cogito

Lacan returns to the unary trait. Identification cannot be understood as the fusion of a subject with a complete image or essence. The decisive mark is the One that counts, repeats, and differentiates. The unary trait is not one object among others. It is the mark through which a series becomes possible.

He uses the Cartesian cogito as a point of contrast. “I am thinking” and “I am” cannot be treated as a seamless identity. The supposed unity of the cogito conceals a division. Lacan writes a formal relation on the board in which the repetition of the One is set against the divided articulation of thinking and being. The important point is not a metaphysical proof of existence but the way the mark of the One makes repetition possible.

[FORMULA: printed p. 154]
Description: Lacan places a fractional expression beginning with `1/(1+1)` alongside a divided formulation of the cogito, visually separating “I am one” from the chain “I am thinking = therefore I am one.” The page uses the spatial arrangement to stress division rather than identity.
Interpretive note: the formula is treated here descriptively because its layout, not a single linear equation, carries the argument.

Lacan's claim is that the unary trait is never truly alone. Once there is a One, its repetition introduces difference. Repetition is not the return of an identical unit without remainder. The second mark repeats the first but, by doing so, creates a sequence in which position and difference appear.

#### Euclid, proportion, and the Fibonacci series

To formalize this, Lacan turns to proportion and the Fibonacci series. He notes that Euclidean demonstration depends on symbolic relations rather than on mere visual intuition. The important point for him is that the formal structure can produce an exact relation not reducible to resemblance.

He then writes a continued fraction associated with the proportional mean, the relation commonly linked to the golden number:

```text
          1
---------------------  = gamma
1 +      1
    -------------
    1 +  1
        -------
        1 + 1
```

[FORMULA: printed p. 156]
Description: a finite displayed segment of the continued fraction that, as extended, generates the proportional mean. Lacan links it to the Fibonacci series `1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...`.

He stresses that the ratio generated by successive Fibonacci terms approaches a limit. The mathematical interest for him lies in the fact that repetition produces a determinate remainder and a relation that is not obvious at the start.

The object `a` is then linked to this formal economy. Lacan writes:

```text
1
--- = a
1+a
```

[FORMULA: printed p. 157]

He also writes a further nested form showing how the same `a` reappears through repetition:

```text
        1
---------------- = a
    1
a + ---
    a+1
```

[FORMULA: printed p. 157]

The mathematical presentation is not offered as a proof that object `a` is literally a number. Lacan uses the recurrence to show a structural feature: repetition produces a remainder that can reappear at another level and that cannot be eliminated by simply continuing the series.

#### Repetition, debt, and Mehrlust

This recurrence lets Lacan return to surplus-jouissance. Repetition is not free. The entry of the One into a series generates a cost, a debt, and a remainder. Lacan connects this to the term *Mehrlust*, surplus-jouissance, whose relation to Marx's surplus-value had been developed earlier in the seminar.

The point is not to identify psychoanalysis with political economy. It is to show that the signifying operation produces something extra and something lost at the same time. The object `a` names the remainder of this operation. In the discourse structures, it occupies different places, but its status as produced remainder remains central.

Lacan's repeated use of the Fibonacci relation clarifies why `a` is not a positive object that existed before discourse and was then hidden. It is an effect of the operation itself. The cause emerges with the effect. The discourse does not simply describe a pre-existing object; it produces the structural remainder that then functions as cause.

#### Science, knowledge, and the exclusion of truth

The chapter then shifts from formal repetition to the historical discourse of science. Lacan distinguishes science from a cumulative store of observations. Modern science is marked by a specific relation to formalization, number, and writing. It is not founded on an original lived experience that is later translated into symbols.

This gives science a peculiar relation to truth. Scientific knowledge can expand without a subject who consciously knows the totality of what science knows. The knowledge functions in formulas, instruments, procedures, and inscriptions. No individual consciousness contains the whole field.

Lacan's emphasis on the autonomy of scientific knowledge parallels his earlier account of unconscious knowledge: knowledge can function without being possessed by a centered subject. But the two are not identical. The unconscious speaks through signifiers and symptoms; science formalizes by excluding or suspending the speaking subject from the place of guarantee.

The result is an enormous expansion of effective knowledge. Scientific discourse produces effects in the world that do not depend on ordinary experience or common sense. The products of science return to social life as objects that reorganize desire, consumption, and the environment of the speaking being.

#### The alethosphere and the lathouses

Lacan names the field produced by modern science the *alethosphere*. The term invokes truth, but the point is not that the modern world has become transparent. On the contrary, scientific truth is materialized in a field of devices, signals, calculations, and objects whose functioning exceeds ordinary understanding.

Within this alethosphere appear what Lacan calls *lathouses*. These are small objects produced by scientific and technological discourse, objects that populate contemporary life and offer themselves to desire. They are not simply neutral tools. They are tied to the circulation of object `a`, to surplus-jouissance, and to the market organization of satisfaction.

Lacan's examples concern the increasingly dense environment of manufactured and technically mediated objects. The world is no longer merely inhabited by natural things and human artifacts in the traditional sense. It is traversed by objects whose existence depends on scientific formalization, industrial production, and networks of exchange.

The neologism matters because Lacan does not want to call these objects simply commodities or gadgets and thereby reduce the argument to economics. Their emergence is tied to the scientific manipulation of the real. They are effects of a discourse that can produce objects whose functioning does not require the user to understand the knowledge embodied in them.

#### Truth, half-saying, and the real

The alethosphere does not eliminate the distinction between truth and the real. Lacan continues to maintain that truth can only be half-said. A scientific formula may function rigorously, but truth in the analytic sense is not exhausted by complete formal knowledge.

The real appears at the level of impossibility. This formulation becomes increasingly important at the end of the chapter. The real is not the totality of what exists outside language. It is what resists formalization at a structural point, what appears as impossible within the articulation itself.

This is also why the analyst's position cannot be reduced to being an expert in the alethosphere. The analyst encounters a subject whose speech, anxiety, desire, and jouissance do not disappear merely because science can produce increasingly powerful knowledge. The analytic relation begins where the subject is caught in a discourse and where the remainder of that discourse cannot be converted into complete knowledge.

The chapter closes by moving toward the distinction between impotence and impossibility, which will become the central axis of Chapter XII.

Session date: 20 May 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter XI, “Furrows in the alethosphere,” printed pp. 150-163.

### XII. The impotence of truth

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter XII, printed pp. 164-179. Session dated 10 June 1970.

#### Examination, teaching, and the demand to know

Lacan begins in the immediate institutional setting of final examinations. The circumstance is not incidental. The university is one of the seminar's principal examples of a discourse in which knowledge occupies the dominant position. Examinations dramatize the demand that knowledge be displayed, certified, measured, and converted into institutional value.

He remarks on the difficulty of knowing what students are asking for and what an institution is doing when it claims to evaluate them. The point is not simply that examinations are unfair or bureaucratic. The examination reveals a structural problem: the institution treats knowledge as something that can be possessed, transmitted, and certified, while psychoanalysis insists that knowledge also functions unconsciously and that truth cannot be exhausted by what a subject can state on demand.

The discussion of teaching therefore remains linked to discourse. Lacan does not present himself as a professor who can guarantee the analyst through instruction. Psychoanalytic formation cannot be reduced to acquiring a body of propositions and then receiving certification that one has mastered them.

#### Vincennes and the institutional question of psychoanalysis

Lacan refers to Vincennes and to invitations and requests connected with teaching psychoanalysis there. He recalls Freud's “Analysis Terminable and Interminable” and the question of what it means to form analysts. The institutional desire to create courses, departments, or credentials for psychoanalysis runs immediately into the problem of analytic discourse itself.

If psychoanalysis is installed as a university subject in the ordinary sense, it risks being transformed into university discourse. Knowledge `S2` becomes agent, addresses an object placed in the position of work, and produces a divided subject. The institution can teach psychoanalytic propositions while structurally occupying a discourse distinct from analytic discourse.

Lacan does not infer that psychoanalysis must therefore avoid institutions altogether. He insists instead on distinguishing the discourses. The same vocabulary can function differently depending on the places occupied by knowledge, truth, object, subject, and master signifier.

#### Capitalism and the mutation of the master's discourse

Lacan then returns to the modern mutation of the master's discourse. Work has acquired an unprecedented value. Modern society does not merely tolerate work as a necessity; it organizes an entire moral and institutional field around production, productivity, and the obligation to work.

He links this to what he calls the capitalist style of the master's discourse. Capitalism is not presented here through a complete economic theory. Lacan isolates a transformation in the relation among mastery, knowledge, work, and surplus. Knowledge is increasingly incorporated into production and administration. The university participates in this circulation.

He asks how far capitalist society can afford a relaxation of university discourse. Reform, protest, and institutional change can occur, but they do not necessarily leave the discourse structure. A reform may simply rearrange the same positions.

The problem is therefore not solved by changing personnel or slogans. One has to ask which term acts as agent, what truth supports it, who or what is put to work, and what is produced.

#### The discourse apparatus

Lacan restates the discourse mechanism explicitly. On printed p. 169 he gives several of the four-discourse arrangements and then abstracts the common places:

```text
UNIVERSITY                  MASTER

   S2  ->  a                  S1  ->  S2
   --      --                 --      --
   S1      $                  $       a

ANALYST                    GENERAL PLACES

   a   ->  $               agent  ->  work
   --      --              -----      ----------
   S2      S1              truth      production
```

[FORMULA / SCHEMA: printed p. 169]

The key distinction is between terms and places. `S1`, `S2`, `$`, and `a` rotate, but the four places remain: agent, truth, work, production. This is why the discourses cannot be reduced to four kinds of persons. The same term takes on a different function when it moves to another place.

Lacan compares the structure to an apparatus, something that can be turned, assembled, tightened, or used as a lever. The metaphor stresses the operational character of the formalism. A discourse is not an essence. It is a machine-like relation among places.

#### Hegel, mastery, and the agent

The term “agent” does not mean that the upper-left place is occupied by a sovereign person who freely causes everything. Lacan explicitly warns against this reading. The agent is a structural position.

This lets him return to Hegel. The Hegelian master does not master by omniscient calculation. The master's position is sustained by a relation to the slave's knowledge and labor. The discourse formula lets Lacan isolate the mechanism without assuming that the empirical master understands it.

He also reopens the question of Kojève's reading of Hegel and of the historical narrative in which mastery is supposedly overcome. Lacan is skeptical of any account in which the contradiction is simply resolved and the structure disappears. The modern university and capitalist organization show that mastery can mutate rather than vanish.

#### Oedipus, desire, and truth as impotence

The chapter then moves from institutional and Hegelian themes back to Freud. Lacan again questions the function of Oedipus and the paternal myth. The truth of the subject is not a complete story that can finally be said without remainder. Truth appears through formations that are partial, distorted, and bound to desire.

This is where the title “The impotence of truth” becomes precise. Truth is not impotent because it is false or weak. Its impotence is structural: truth cannot command the whole discourse from a position of complete effectiveness. In the discourse formulas, truth is beneath the agent, separated from direct mastery.

Lacan increasingly distinguishes impotence from impossibility. Impotence is experienced at the level of a failed relation: something cannot be done, achieved, or completed. Impossibility is stronger. It designates a structural nonrelation, a point that cannot be written within the system as a successful relation.

The distinction matters clinically. A subject can interpret a structural impossibility as a personal impotence and then organize complaint, guilt, or fantasy around the belief that someone else could succeed where the subject fails. Analysis has to separate these levels.

#### The analyst, the impossible, and object a

Lacan returns to the analyst's discourse. The analyst takes the place of `a`, not the place of the master who knows. This is why the analyst cannot guarantee truth by authority. The analyst functions as cause, setting the divided subject to work in speech.

The impossibility at stake in analysis is not a technical obstacle that a more skillful analyst will someday remove. It belongs to the structure of the relation between signifier and jouissance. The subject cannot recover a complete object that would abolish division.

Lacan connects this to the impossibility of the sexual relation. The phrase is not yet developed in the full form it will receive later, but the structural direction is already clear. Language does not supply a signifier that would write a complete complementary relation between the sexes. What appears instead are substitutions, fantasies, identifications, and objects `a`.

The distinction between impotence and impossibility therefore becomes a way to read symptoms and social institutions alike. Institutions repeatedly present structural impossibilities as problems that could be solved with enough knowledge, reform, or efficiency. Analysis asks whether the supposed defect is actually the effect of a relation that cannot be completed.

#### University production and the divided subject

The chapter closes by returning to university discourse. Knowledge in the place of agent addresses `a`, and the divided subject is produced. The student is not simply a passive victim. The discourse produces a subject whose division can itself become a site of protest, dissatisfaction, and demand for another master.

This is why student revolt does not automatically escape the university structure. A revolt can demand a new master signifier and thereby rotate back toward another form of mastery. Lacan's formalism is intended to make this danger visible without reducing the political situation to a moral judgment on students.

The movement of Chapter XII prepares the final chapter: if truth is structurally impotent and the real is approached through impossibility, then the question becomes how the impossible functions as a source of power within discourse rather than simply as a limit.

Session date: 10 June 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter XII, “The impotence of truth,” printed pp. 164-179.

### XIII. The power of the impossibles

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter XIII, printed pp. 180-193. Session dated 17 June 1970. Printed pp. 194-196 are transition/divider matter before the Appendixes.

#### Shame as the opening problem

Lacan opens the final seminar session with shame. He says that it is not useless to speak about shame and treats the question as a diagnostic one for contemporary discourse. Shame is not introduced as a moral virtue to be restored by preaching. It is an affect that reveals a relation to the Other, to exposure, to the gaze, and to the master signifier.

He refers to student interventions and to the atmosphere around Vincennes. The challenge is not merely whether students should or should not feel shame. The question is what happens to shame in a social bond in which traditional master signifiers have weakened, knowledge has become increasingly autonomous, and enjoyment is publicly organized and circulated.

Lacan's use of shame therefore belongs to the discourse theory. Shame appears when the subject is caught in a relation to a signifier and to the Other's gaze, not simply when an internal moral conscience condemns an action.

#### Hegel, culture, and the spectacle of mastery

The discussion moves through Hegel and the relation between master and slave. Lacan again resists a triumphalist story in which history simply abolishes mastery. The contemporary situation may change the signs of authority while preserving the structural relation between knowledge, labor, and surplus.

He is especially attentive to the way culture packages critique. A discourse can absorb its own opposition. What presents itself as subversion can become another product, another cultural object, or another route through which the same structure reproduces itself.

This is why Lacan distrusts appeals to consciousness alone. Making everyone aware of domination does not automatically change the places in the discourse. The structural operation can continue under a new vocabulary.

#### University production: the divided subject

Lacan returns to the university discourse and draws a rectangular diagram. The four terms occupy the corners:

```text
S2 ---------------- a
| \              / |
|   \          /   |
|     \      /     |
|       \  /       |
|       /  \       |
|     /      \     |
|   /          \   |
| /              \ |
S1 ---------------- $
```

[FIGURE: printed p. 184]
Description: a rectangle with `S2` at the upper left, `a` at the upper right, `S1` at the lower left, and `$` at the lower right, crossed by two diagonals.
Interpretive note: Lacan says that, if one thing is retained from the year's work, attention should be paid to the level of production in the university system. In the university discourse, the product is the divided subject `$`.

The figure condenses the entire seminar's method. Knowledge `S2` acts as agent, supported by `S1` in the place of truth, addresses `a` as work, and produces `$`. The university does not merely transmit neutral information. It produces a form of subjectivity.

Lacan's concern is not that every professor consciously intends this result. The discourse functions independently of individual intention. A student may resist the institution while still being produced within the same formal relation.

#### Knowledge and truth are not complementary virtues

Lacan then reads from a response he had given to an interlocutor who asked about knowledge and truth. The question assumes that knowledge and truth might be two compatible goods that could finally be brought together. Lacan rejects this.

Truth is not a stable partner with which knowledge can enter into a contract. He describes truth as seductive, deceptive, and structurally resistant to possession. Psychoanalysis does not promise a final marriage between complete knowledge and complete truth.

This is why the analyst must be cautious about the fantasy of knowing the patient's truth. The analyst who believes he possesses it becomes captive to the very mastery analytic discourse is supposed to displace. The proper analytic position leaves room for truth to emerge in speech without converting the analyst into its owner.

The relation between knowledge and truth is therefore a nonrelation in the strong sense. Knowledge can expand indefinitely; truth appears in cuts, slips, symptoms, and half-sayings. Neither can simply absorb the other.

#### Culture, mass media, and the circulation of discourse

Lacan also reflects on the transmission of discourse through radio and mass media. A statement can circulate at a level where the speaker does not control how it is received. This does not necessarily degrade the discourse. It can expose the fact that meaning is never guaranteed by authorial intention.

He questions the paternalistic assumption that a broad audience must always be addressed at a lower intellectual level. Culture often justifies simplification by presuming the incompetence of the public. Lacan reverses the problem: the apparent need to lower the level may itself be an effect of the cultural system one claims merely to accommodate.

The issue is continuous with the university discussion. Institutions define who is supposed to know, who is supposed not to know, and how knowledge should circulate. Analytic discourse disturbs these assignments because it starts from knowledge that is not mastered by the subject who speaks.

#### The real as impossible

The chapter's central theoretical claim is that the real is approached through the impossible. Lacan states that the real is not simply what lies outside discourse as a positive thing. It is what cannot be written as a successful relation within the symbolic structure.

This is why the impossible has power. It is not merely a negative boundary where thought stops. An impossibility organizes the entire field around it. The fact that a relation cannot be completed produces substitutions, repetitions, symptoms, inventions, and discourses.

Lacan uses the four-discourse structure as an example. Each discourse is defined not only by what it permits but also by the impossible relation built into its arrangement. The barriers and failures are constitutive. They are not accidental malfunctions waiting for a perfect system to remove them.

This logic also clarifies the difference between impossibility and impotence established in Chapter XII. Impotence is experienced as failure. Impossibility is structural and can therefore generate effects repeatedly. The impossible is powerful precisely because it cannot be eliminated by success.

#### The quadruped and the four places

Lacan calls the discourse schema his little quadruped. The four-legged structure is not a metaphor for four psychological types. It is a formal device for tracking how the same terms change function when they move through agent, truth, work, and production.

He returns to the rotation of `S1`, `S2`, `$`, and `a` and to the fact that no position can be understood independently of the others. Knowledge becomes mastery in one place, hidden truth in another. The divided subject can be agent in the hysteric's discourse and product in the university discourse. Object `a` can be product in the master's discourse and agent in analytic discourse.

The power of the schema lies in showing how a social bond is organized by an impossibility rather than by a shared substance. This is also why the discourses can change historically without the underlying problem of the real disappearing.

#### Shame, the gaze, and contemporary enjoyment

Lacan returns to shame in the final movement. Shame has a relation to being seen, but not merely to visual perception. It concerns the subject's exposure in the field of the Other. A subject can be caught by a gaze that reveals the inadequacy of the signifier under which the subject presents itself.

The contemporary weakening of shame is therefore not simply moral decline. It can indicate a transformation in the social bond. A discourse increasingly organized around the public circulation of enjoyment may no longer rely on the same forms of concealment and prohibition. What once produced shame may be displayed, marketed, or converted into spectacle.

Lacan does not celebrate this as liberation. Nor does he call for a return to traditional morality. His concern is structural: what happens to the subject when the relation between master signifier, knowledge, and jouissance changes?

The issue connects back to surplus-jouissance. Contemporary discourse can command enjoyment while simultaneously multiplying the objects through which enjoyment is pursued. The lathouses of the previous chapter and the university production of the divided subject belong to the same field.

#### Psychoanalysis and the refusal of mastery

The final pages return implicitly to the ethical position of analysis. Psychoanalysis cannot resolve the impossible by promising a complete knowledge of the subject. Nor can it simply reject knowledge. Analytic discourse places knowledge in the position of truth and object `a` in the position of agent, thereby refusing the fantasy that the analyst is the master who knows.

This refusal is difficult because institutions continually pull psychoanalysis back toward mastery and university discourse. Training, certification, teaching, publication, and professional authority all create pressures to convert analytic knowledge into a body of authorized doctrine.

Lacan's discourse theory does not claim that psychoanalysis can stand outside all institutions. It supplies a way to identify the discourse operating at a given moment and to notice when the analyst's position has been replaced by that of the master or professor.

#### Closing the seminar: impossibility as structural leverage

The seminar closes without a synthesis that would dissolve its tensions. The four discourses remain distinct but related by rotation. Truth remains half-said. Knowledge remains separable from the subject who speaks it. Jouissance appears as both loss and surplus. The master's discourse mutates into modern forms rather than disappearing. The university becomes one of the principal sites in which knowledge operates as command. Analytic discourse depends on occupying a structurally different position.

The final emphasis on impossibility provides the strongest unifying thread. What cannot be written or completed is not inert. It organizes desire, discourse, social bonds, and analytic work. The impossible is therefore not the end of the analysis but the point around which an analysis can distinguish structural limit from fantasies of personal failure.

Session date: 17 June 1970.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Chapter XIII, “The power of the impossibles,” printed pp. 180-193; printed pp. 194-196 are transition/divider matter before Appendix A.

## APPENDIXES

### A. Analyticon

Source location: Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Appendix A, printed pp. 197-208.

Session location and date: Vincennes experimental university, 3 December 1969.

The appendix records an unusually contentious public session at the experimental university at Vincennes. It is explicitly framed as the first of four projected impromptus under the title "Analyticon." The printed subheads signal the course of the exchange: the agitator who prepares his own chocolate; the impasse of psychoanalytic selection; credit points; the proposition that nothing is everything; and the spectacle of people "doing it." Unlike the regular seminar chapters, the appendix is dialogical from the outset. Anonymous interventions from the audience interrupt Lacan repeatedly and must be kept distinct from his replies.

#### Vincennes as an experiment and the reappearance of the four discourses

Lacan opens by speaking about his dog, Justine, whom he also jokingly casts as an Egeria. The anecdote is not a digression without function. The dog, he says, knows what she is saying without saying it in words, and her chief deficit in comparison with the people around him is that she has not been to university. The joke moves directly into the institutional setting. Lacan presents Vincennes as an experiment and announces that he intends to use it to continue the articulation of the four discourse positions begun in the seminar.

He first recalls the master's discourse and then turns to the hysteric's discourse, stressing that the latter matters because psychoanalytic discourse takes shape from it. An audience member objects that there are no psychoanalysts at Vincennes and asks why students should be expected to become psychoanalysts after receiving teaching. Lacan answers that psychoanalysis cannot be transmitted simply as one transmits a body of knowledge. The analyst certainly occupies a position in relation to discourse, but this does not mean that a stock of knowledge is simply handed over from teacher to pupil.

The distinction lets Lacan reintroduce the elementary discourse notation. He places on the board the familiar master's arrangement:

```text
S1 -> S2
$     a
```

The signifier represents a subject for another signifier. Lacan treats this notation as the starting point for a formal chain rather than as a picture of social personalities. He links it to the problem of the psychoanalyst's position and to the psychoanalytic act, asking how someone comes one day to commit himself to being a psychoanalyst. The difficulty is not merely training in a technical sense. It concerns a selection process and a transformation of position that cannot be guaranteed by institutional transmission alone.

#### The psychoanalytic act and the impasse of institutional selection

Lacan recalls having suspended his seminar on the psychoanalytic act before the end of 1968 and links the present agitation to the unresolved problem of what the act implies. He jokes with Marcel Duchamp's phrase about the bachelor preparing his own chocolate, warning that the agitator may likewise be preparing his own chocolate. The point is polemical but structural: agitation can imagine itself outside the institution while repeating the logic it denounces.

He then refers to debates within psychoanalytic institutions and to writings criticizing their selection procedures. His concern is not to defend an existing institution as such. Rather, he argues that the existence of the psychoanalyst raises a problem that the institutions responsible for authorizing analysts can easily cover over. A selection procedure may become masterly precisely where it claims merely to certify competence. The psychoanalyst's position cannot be reduced to an institutional title or to successful completion of a curriculum.

This argument provokes a series of interventions accusing Lacan of criticizing psychoanalysis obliquely, refusing direct self-criticism, or setting himself up as the privileged person who can speak while others cannot. Lacan repeatedly distinguishes his structural claims from a denunciation of psychoanalysis as such. The exchanges make the appendix less a lecture than a live demonstration of competing discourses struggling over who may speak, who knows, and who authorizes whom.

#### Credit points and the university discourse

The discussion turns to credit points. Lacan takes them as a concrete entry into the university discourse. An audience member insists that the local struggle is not about credits but about psychoanalysis; Lacan replies that people evidently care very much about credits and uses the board to situate the point formally.

In the university discourse, `S2`, knowledge, occupies the upper-left or agent position. The discourse is obtained by a quarter-turn from the master's discourse. Knowledge operates as command, while the student is placed at the site of the object produced and exploited. Lacan ties this to his earlier use of Marx: object `a` is treated as surplus-jouissance in a structural relation analogous to surplus value. Students who leave the institution stamped with credit points can thus be understood, provocatively, as products of a machinery in which knowledge functions as authority.

The students object that this account mythologizes the situation and that Lacan is himself reproducing the authority he describes. The resulting quarrel is part of the evidence of the appendix. At one moment an intervenor removes his shirt. Lacan responds mockingly, while other speakers reproach him for making the audience laugh and for reducing political criticism to spectacle. The scene repeatedly shifts between theory and enactment, with the audience contesting not only Lacan's propositions but his control of the situation.

#### Four letters, incompleteness, and "nothing is everything"

When Lacan manages to resume the thread, he defines his project as the articulation of a weak but effective logic composed of four little letters. Its importance lies in the incompleteness it formalizes. Each four-legged discourse schema leaves a gap. The discourses do not totalize the social bond into a closed system.

For the master's discourse, the gap appears in the recuperation of surplus value. For the university discourse, a different gap appears. Lacan insists that the problem is not that the knowledge taught at the university is simply false, incoherent, or unstructured. The university can possess organized knowledge while still binding teachers and students into a structure of work, production, and surplus value.

He condenses the logical point in the formula that "nothing is everything". The phrase refuses the fantasy that some position outside the system could finally gather the whole and master it. The gap is not a temporary defect waiting for sufficient revolutionary knowledge. It belongs to the structure of the discourse itself.

The hysteric's discourse then enters the argument historically. Lacan says that it made possible a decisive shift in the interpretation of historical events by allowing them to be read as symptoms. He links this movement to Marx and then to the emergence of psychoanalytic discourse from listening to hysterical speech. The hysteric calls for a master who will know, but the analyst's discourse does not answer by installing a final knowing master. The limit appears in castration, which Lacan names as the point at which the joke about total knowledge stops.

#### Revolution, leaving the university, and the persistence of discourse

The third major phase of the session is driven by political interventions. Students point to actions outside the university, including Beaux-Arts students taking their teaching elsewhere and militants seeking alliances with workers and peasants. They ask Lacan to say whether the university must be left and destroyed from outside.

Lacan does not accept the spatial opposition between inside and outside as sufficient. When one leaves the university one continues speaking, and therefore remains within language and discourse. To get people to leave, one may first have to enter. This is not an argument that institutions cannot change. It is an argument that no political exit abolishes the structural problem merely by crossing a physical boundary.

He sharpens the point with the Soviet Union. Against the idea that a workers-and-peasants configuration automatically escapes university logic, Lacan says that in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics the university occupies the driving seat. Knowledge is king. The audience protests that he is substituting one political society for another, but Lacan's point is that a revolution can transform ownership and institutions while still producing a discourse in which knowledge takes command.

Asked whether psychoanalysis would have a function in a new society, Lacan refuses to define society by an ideal image of its future organization. What dominates a society, he says, is the practice of language. He invokes aphasia to make the dependence on language concrete: the breakdown of the capacity to manage language produces a profound incapacity, showing that language is not a superficial layer added to a social substance.

From this he derives the appendix's most pointed statement about revolution. Revolutionary aspiration has, in his view, a recurrent outcome: it ends in the master's discourse. What revolutionaries aspire to is a master, and they will get one. An audience member names Pompidou; Lacan rejects the simplification and returns to the problem of discourse rather than personalities.

#### The final provocation: "Look at them enjoying"

Lacan closes by playing with the word "liberal" and describing himself as liberal only insofar as he is anti-progressive, while simultaneously being caught in a movement that deserves to be called progressive insofar as psychoanalytic discourse is being founded. That discourse, he says, completes a circle that may allow one to locate more precisely what rebellion is directed against without supposing that rebellion itself automatically escapes the structure.

He then turns the Vincennes experiment back upon the audience. The students, he says provocatively, fulfill the role of helots for the regime. The regime can put them on display and say, in effect, "Look at them enjoying." The institution can therefore incorporate contestation itself as spectacle. The session ends abruptly with Lacan saying goodbye.

The appendix is important because it displays the discourse theory under conditions of live antagonism. The four discourses are not applied as personality types to the students. Instead, Lacan uses the conflict to show how mastery, knowledge, divided subjectivity, surplus-jouissance, institutional authorization, and revolutionary demand can change places while remaining structurally connected.

Session date: 3 December 1969.

#### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Appendix A, "Analyticon," printed pp. 197-208.

### B. Monsieur Caquot's presentation

Source location: *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, Appendix B, printed pp. 209-213.

Speaker/author attribution: the appendix is explicitly titled "Monsieur Caquot's presentation" and is reconstructed here as André Caquot's scholarly presentation, not as Lacan's discourse.

#### Purpose of the presentation

Caquot's presentation supplies the philological background to Freud's use of Ernst Sellin in *Moses and Monotheism*. Freud appealed to Sellin as an authority for the proposition that Moses may have been killed by his own people. Caquot therefore asks what Sellin actually argued, how he constructed the argument from Hosea, and how secure the underlying exegesis was.

He begins by situating Sellin historically. Sellin, born in 1867, belonged to the German exegetical tradition and in 1922 published a book on Moses and the meaning of Moses for Israelite and Jewish religious history. Caquot stresses both Sellin's ideological and methodological commitments. Ideologically, Sellin stood within liberal Protestantism and treated the moral preaching associated with the Ten Commandments and the eighth-century prophets as a high point of biblical revelation. He regarded Moses as the founder of Israel's religion, author of the commandments, and initiator of the moral tradition that the prophets continued. On this model, prophetic traditions could preserve traces of Moses' life that later historical or priestly narratives had suppressed.

Methodologically, Sellin was willing to distrust the Masoretic Hebrew text and to prefer ancient versions or conjectural emendations when the received text seemed obscure. Caquot notes that this style of exegesis could become highly inventive. The murder hypothesis depends precisely on a chain of such emendations.

#### Hosea 5:2, Shittim, and the reconstruction of a murder

The first major passage is Hosea 5:2. The received wording is obscure. Earlier scholarship had proposed replacing an unclear term with the place-name Shittim. Sellin adopted the conjecture and connected it to Numbers 25, where Israel is at Shittim and the episode of Baal of Peor leads to plague, sexual transgression, and the killing performed by Phinehas.

Sellin goes much further than the textual correction itself warrants. He reconstructs the victim behind the biblical story as Moses. Moses' Midianite or Moabite marriage becomes part of the conjectural background. The later priestly story, on Sellin's account, rewrites the event so that Phinehas becomes the zealous hero, while the names Zimri and Cozbi replace figures in an earlier account centered on Moses. Moses' death is thereby read as an expiatory sacrifice connected with the collective sin at Baal of Peor.

Caquot's reconstruction makes clear how many inferential steps separate the obscure prophetic phrase from the claim that Moses was murdered. The interest is not that the hypothesis is simply absurd, but that it emerges from a particular philological practice in which difficult Hebrew is repeatedly emended until it supports a historical scenario.

#### Hosea 9:9 and the second Shittim reconstruction

Sellin also works on Hosea 9:9, another indictment of Ephraim. By altering the vocalization and related elements, he again tries to recover Shittim and an image of a pit or grave. A passage normally associated with the "days of Gibeah" is reorganized so that it appears to contain a hidden reference to the burial or killing of Moses.

Caquot emphasizes the cumulative character of the procedure. The second passage does not independently prove the first. Rather, once the murder hypothesis has been adopted, textual obscurities are read as further encrypted traces of the same event. The reconstruction thus acquires apparent coherence through repeated conjectural correction.

#### Hosea 12-13 and the expiatory prophet

A third set of passages concerns Hosea 12:13-13:1, where Moses is unambiguously evoked through the prophet by whom Israel was brought out of Egypt and tended. Sellin again modifies wording and sequence in order to produce a scenario in which the prophet bears guilt or punishment for the people and dies in relation to the Baal of Peor episode.

Caquot notes the Christian background to this reading. Sellin's Moses begins to resemble the suffering or expiatory figure familiar from Christian readings of prophetic texts. The hypothesis is therefore not merely a neutral recovery of an ancient event. It is shaped by theological expectations about martyrdom, sacrifice, and the suffering servant.

#### Sellin's later revisions and the fragility of the hypothesis

Caquot then follows Sellin's own revisions. Sellin was aware that the 1922 construction was fragile. In later work he continued to revisit the Hosea passages, but altered some of the emendations and became more skeptical about the exact textual basis on which he had originally rested the murder thesis. In the later edition of his Hosea commentary he abandoned or modified important parts of the earlier reconstruction, even if he did not immediately abandon every form of the idea that a violent death of Moses might lie behind prophetic tradition.

The presentation closes by widening the scholarly context. Caquot notes that the idea of a murdered Moses was not unique to Sellin and mentions an earlier speculative proposal by Goethe in which Joshua and Caleb kill the aged Moses before entry into the promised land. That comparison does not establish a historical event. It instead underlines how readily a narrative possibility can circulate independently of adequate evidence. Caquot's final thrust is methodological: the surviving texts do not provide a secure basis for reconstructing the murder of Moses with the confidence that Freud's use of Sellin might suggest.

This appendix therefore clarifies Chapter IX without settling Lacan's broader argument. Caquot's contribution is philological and historical. It shows that the Sellin hypothesis rests on a sequence of conjectural emendations whose evidentiary force is weak and whose theological presuppositions matter. It should not be rewritten as a proposition by Lacan.

#### Sources used

- André Caquot, "Monsieur Caquot's presentation," Appendix B in Jacques Lacan, *Seminar XVII: The Other Side of Psychoanalysis*, printed pp. 209-213.

## Key terms appearing in this file

- **Agent**: the upper-left structural place from which a discourse operates; not simply the psychological person who happens to speak.
- **Alethosphere**: Lacan's neologism for the technologically saturated sphere associated with modern science, transmission, and truth-effects.
- **Analyst discourse**: the discourse in which object `a` occupies the agent position, addressing the divided subject and placing knowledge in the position of truth.
- **Barred/divided subject (`$`)**: the subject divided by the signifier and represented within the discourse structures.
- **Castration**: treated structurally through the signifier, prohibition, jouissance, the father, and the impossibility organizing the sexual field rather than as a merely anatomical event.
- **Discourse**: a formal social bond articulated through four places and four terms rather than a style of speaking or a personality type.
- **Hysteric discourse**: the discourse in which the divided subject addresses the master signifier and drives the production of knowledge.
- **Jouissance**: enjoyment beyond simple pleasure, bound in the seminar to loss, repetition, prohibition, body, discourse, and surplus.
- **Knowledge (`S2`, *savoir*)**: signifying articulation that can function independently of conscious knowing and occupies different structural places in different discourses.
- **Lathouse**: one of Lacan's fabricated terms for objects generated within the scientific-technological and commodity environment of the alethosphere.
- **Master discourse**: the discourse in which `S1` addresses `S2`, producing object `a` while the divided subject occupies the place of truth beneath the master signifier.
- **Master signifier (`S1`)**: the signifier that occupies the commanding or organizing place in the master discourse and is repeatedly contrasted with articulated knowledge `S2`.
- **Myth**: a mode of half-saying that Lacan contrasts with formal structural articulation in his rereading of Oedipus, Moses, and the primal father.
- **Object `a`**: remainder/cause tied to loss and jouissance; in analyst discourse it occupies the agent position.
- **Other**: the locus or treasury of signifiers, implicated in knowledge, truth, and the subject's relation to discourse.
- **Plus-de-jouir / surplus-jouissance**: the surplus produced through the signifying operation, developed by analogy with Marxian surplus value without being reducible to economics.
- **Real**: especially where impossibility, the father, jouissance, or the failure of complete formalization is at stake.
- **Repetition**: linked to the unary trait, loss of jouissance, knowledge, and the production of surplus.
- **Shame**: a central late-seminar affect used to address visibility, the gaze, degradation of the social bond, and contemporary relations to enjoyment.
- **Truth**: structurally placed beneath the agent, resistant to complete statement and repeatedly formulated through half-saying rather than total knowledge.
- **University discourse**: the discourse in which `S2` occupies the commanding position and acts upon object `a`, producing the divided subject.

## Provenance / source note

The substantive reconstruction in this file derives only from the project source `lacan-seminar-17-the-other-side-of-psychoanalysis-en.pdf`, the Russell Grigg English translation of Seminar XVII edited by Jacques-Alain Miller. It is a detailed reconstruction and not Lacan's verbatim text. The seminar's primary argument has been paraphrased in source order, while important formulas, spatial schemas, named references, supplements, and session structures have been retained as faithfully as the scan permits.

Russell Grigg's Translator's Note is explicitly attributed to Grigg. Anonymous interventions in Chapter X and Appendix A are kept distinct from Lacan's replies. Appendix B is André Caquot's presentation and is not represented as Lacan's own discourse. Editorial, translator, audience, and quoted-author voices are not silently merged into Lacan.

No secondary Seminar XVII companion, no Seminar XVI source, no Écrits source, no Fink/Soler/Miller/Zupančič commentary, no dictionary, and no web source was used to fill substantive gaps. Freud, Hegel, Marx, biblical texts, Sellin, Wittgenstein, Sade, Kierkegaard, Castoriadis, and other figures appear only as they are mobilized within this Seminar XVII source.

## Processing notes and uncertainties

The source is a 111-scan-page image-based PDF containing many two-page spreads. Production therefore used visible printed page numbers and chapter headings rather than assuming a fixed mapping between scan-page numbers and printed pagination.

No global OCR was used. Chunks A-D were reconstructed from direct rendered-page inspection, with targeted high-resolution re-rendering for difficult formulas and figures. Appendix B required one targeted local OCR pass on printed pp. 212-213 to resolve small type concerning Sellin's later revisions and the concluding Goethe comparison; that result was visually checked against the rendered scan. No unresolved substantive source uncertainty remains in the completed reconstruction.

The contents page lists Acknowledgments at printed p. 215, but that page is absent or unrecoverable in the available project scan. No acknowledgment text was invented. The Bibliography at pp. 217-219 and Index at pp. 221-224 were inspected selectively but not transcribed because they are non-argumentative back matter.

### Formal material accounted for

The reconstruction preserves or explicitly describes the seminar's major formal displays encountered in the source:

- p. 13: master-discourse arrangement, `S1 -> S2` over `$` and `a`;
- p. 14: quarter-turn arrangement later identified with hysteric discourse;
- p. 29: four-discourse reference grid, University / Master / Hysteric / Analyst;
- p. 39: repeated four-discourse reference grid opening Chapter III;
- p. 54: discourse display opening Chapter IV;
- p. 69: two-by-two field of the four discourses opening Chapter V;
- p. 93: functional master-discourse schema;
- p. 94: hysteric/master contrast;
- p. 102: positional equivalence `M(S1) ~= U(S2)`;
- p. 104: university-discourse arrangement;
- p. 108: master discourse with lower-level barrier of jouissance;
- p. 130: analyst's discourse at the Chapter VIII close;
- p. 154: divided-cogito/unary-trait layout beginning with `1/(1+1)`;
- p. 156: continued fraction for the proportional mean / Fibonacci series;
- p. 157: `1/(a+1) = a` and recurrence returning `a`;
- p. 169: discourse-place schema involving University, Master, Analyst, agent, truth, work, and production;
- p. 184: university-discourse rectangle with `S2`, `a`, `S1`, and `$`, crossed diagonally;
- p. 198: master-discourse arrangement in Appendix A;
- p. 201: university-discourse board schema in Appendix A.

Where spatial form carries meaning, the body uses monospaced blocks or descriptive representations rather than silently reducing the structure to prose. The four discourses are treated throughout as formal discourse structures and social bonds, not as personality categories.

# Jacques Lacan - Seminar XX: Encore - Part A

## Source and Scope

**Title:** *The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book XX: Encore*  
**Subtitle:** *On Feminine Sexuality: The Limits of Love and Knowledge*  
**Seminar year:** 1972-1973  
**Author:** Jacques Lacan  
**Editor:** Jacques-Alain Miller  
**English translator:** Bruce Fink  
**Publisher:** W. W. Norton & Company  
**Corpus file:** `22_SEMINAR_XX_ENCORE_PART_A.md`  
**Scope:** Bruce Fink's Preface and Chapters I-VI.  
**Continuation:** `23_SEMINAR_XX_ENCORE_PART_B.md` begins with Chapter VII, "A love letter."  
**Source note:** Structured full-text conversion from the project PDF. The source is scan/image based; uncertain readings, if any, are explicitly marked rather than silently reconstructed.

## Preface

### Bruce Fink

This translation is long overdue. Published in French in 1975, this groundbreaking Seminar - including some of Lacan's most sophisticated work on love, desire, and jouissance - could well have appeared in English around the same time as the early *Ecrits: A Selection* (1977) and *The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis* (Seminar XI, 1978). In its absence, Lacan, instead of *presenting himself* to the English-speaking world, has been believed by many to be faithfully presented to us by certain of his one-time students - such as Julia Kristeva and Luce Irigaray, though their views diverge substantially from his on many points - and by a spate of American, Australian, and British critics who have, in my view, grossly misrepresented him.

This translation, long-awaited by the public and by me - I always wanted copies to distribute to students and colleagues, though I never expected to be given the opportunity to translate it *myself* until the day Jacques-Alain Miller and Norton proposed it to me - is thus offered up in the hope of rekindling debate on the basis of something closer to what Lacan actually said, and quieting the kinds of banal reductions of Lacan's views to pat phrases derived from commentaries on commentaries on commentaries that currently pass for serious academic discourse.

I have not deliberately tried to vindicate my own previously published interpretation of Lacan's view of sexual difference in this translation, attempting instead to remain open to being surprised by his formulations (and, indeed, I was surprised!). Nevertheless, Lacan's French is - as anyone who has made a serious attempt to grapple with it is aware - so polyvalent and ambiguous that some frame must be imposed to make any sense of it whatsoever. As is true in the case of an analyst listening to the discourse proffered by an analysand, there is no escaping a theoretical frame of sorts - for without some frame one hears nothing or simply falls back on the ready-made frame provided by pop psychology - and the challenge to the analyst and translator alike is to keep the frame flexible enough to hear what is new, and to keep oneself flexible enough to adjust part or all of the frame accordingly.

The frame I rely on here is, as I hope will be apparent to the reader, the larger context of Lacan's work, including the complete *Ecrits* (the 925 pages of which I am currently translating and retranslating for Norton), virtually all of Lacan's seminars, and other of Lacan's writings and lectures as well. I have striven to make sense of what Lacan says here in the context of what he said before and afterward. His work obviously fits into a historical, philosophical, literary, and psychiatric context as well, all the elements of which no one person could ever hope to master. Russell Grigg (the translator of Seminar III, *The Psychoses*, who is currently translating Seminar XVIII) and Heloise Fink were very helpful in providing such references. Readers of this translation are encouraged to write to me care of the publisher regarding specialized vocabulary and specific works and authors alluded to that I may have overlooked. Adequate translation of Lacan's work is a long-term project to which many people in many fields should contribute.

A word here about my translation "strategy": I have sought to keep the translation itself as "clean" and flowing as possible, and this has led me to relegate some complex phraseology and discussion of alternative readings to the footnotes. It seems to me that the impact of certain passages is easily defused by the inclusion of too many slashes, parenthetical remarks, and unusual typography (of which Lacan himself provides enough). I have endeavored throughout to make the English translation have as powerful an effect on the English reader as the French does on the French, and this can only be obtained by occasionally nailing down meanings more tightly than might be hoped for the purposes of extensive commentary. On such occasions I have dropped footnotes detailing what may well have been lopped off.

I am grateful to Russell Grigg who, in his thorough reading of Chapter I of this translation, reminded me once again of just how many alternative readings are possible. Heloise Fink provided invaluable assistance by checking the *entire* French and English texts line by line and spending countless hours patiently poring over Lacan's quirky grammar and endless ambiguities with me. I alone am responsible for the inaccuracies that inevitably remain.

Certain readers may need to be reminded that this was not a text at all originally, but rather a series of largely improvised talks given from notes. The French editor of the Seminar, Jacques-Alain Miller, had to work from a stenographer's faulty transcription of those talks, and was obliged to invent spellings for certain of Lacan's neologisms and condensations and new ways of punctuating for Lacan's idiosyncratic speech. All of the paragraph breaks here follow the French text, and much of the punctuation here is modeled on that adopted by Miller and approved of by Lacan.

Few texts in the Lacanian opus are as difficult to render into English as this one, given Lacan's myriad word plays and his ever more polyvalent, evocative style. I can only hope - as I have said elsewhere - that my translation here "compensates" the reader for the inevitable loss in plurivocity with *another satisfaction*.

Bruce Fink

## I. On jouissance

It so happened that I did not publish *The Ethics of Psychoanalysis*.[^I-1] At the time, it was a form of politeness on my part - after you, be my guest, be my *worst*....[^I-2] With the passage of time, I learned that I could say a little more about it. And then I realized that what constituted my course was a sort of "I don't want to know anything about it."

That is no doubt why, with the passage of time, I am still *(encore)* here, and you are too. I never cease to be amazed by it....[^I-3]

What has worked in my favor for a while is that there is also on your part, in the great mass of you who are here, an "I don't want to know anything about it." But - the all important question - is it the same one?

Is your "I don't want to know anything about it" regarding a certain knowledge that is transmitted to you bit by bit what is at work in me? I don't think so, and it is precisely because you suppose that I begin from a different place than you in this "I don't want to know anything about it" that you find yourselves attached (*lies*) to me. Such that, while it is true that with respect to you I can only be here in the position of an analysand due to my "I don't want to know anything about it," it'll be quite some time before you reach the same point.

That is why it is only when yours seems adequate to you that you can, if you are one of my analysands, normally detach yourself from your analysis. The conclusion I draw from this is that, contrary to what people have been saying, there is no contradiction between my position as an analyst and what I do here.

### 1

Last year I entitled what I thought I could say to you, ... *ou pire* (... or Worse), and then, *Ca s'oupire*.[^I-4] That has nothing to do with "I" or "you" - *je ne t'oupire pas, ni tu ne m'oupires*. Our path, that of analytic discourse, progresses only due to this narrow limit, this cutting edge of the knife, which is such that elsewhere it can only get worse (*s'oupirer*).

That is the discourse that underpins (*supporte*)[^I-5] my work, and to begin it anew this year, I am first of all going to assume that you are in bed, a bed employed to its fullest, there being two of you in it.

To someone, a jurist, who had been kind enough to inquire about my discourse, I felt I could respond - in order to give him a sense of its foundation, namely, that language[^I-6] is not the speaking being - that I did not feel out of place having to speak in a law school, since it is the school in which the existence of codes makes it clear that language consists therein and is separate, having been constituted over the ages, whereas speaking beings, known as men, are something else altogether. Thus, to begin by assuming that you are in bed requires that I apologize to him.

I won't leave this bed today, and I will remind the jurist that law basically talks about what I am going to talk to you about - jouissance.

Law does not ignore the bed. Take, for example, the fine common law on which the practice of concubinage, which means to sleep together, is based. What I am going to do is begin with what remains veiled in law, namely, what we do in that bed - squeeze each other tight (*s'etreindre*). I begin with the limit, a limit with which one must indeed begin if one is to be serious, in other words, to establish the series of that which approaches it.

A word here to shed light on the relationship between law (*droit*) and jouissance. "Usufruct" - that's a legal notion, isn't it? - brings together in one word what I already mentioned in my seminar on ethics, namely, the difference between utility[^I-7] and jouissance. What purpose does utility serve? That has never been well defined owing to the prodigious respect speaking beings have, due to language, for means. "Usufruct" means that you can enjoy (*jouir de*)[^I-8] your means, but must not waste them. When you have the usufruct of an inheritance, you can enjoy the inheritance (*en jouir*) as long as you don't use up too much of it. That is clearly the essence of law - to divide up, distribute, or reattribute everything that counts as jouissance.

What is jouissance? Here it amounts to no more than a negative instance (*instance*).[^I-9] Jouissance is what serves no purpose (*ne sert a rien*).

I am pointing here to the reservation implied by the field of the right-to-jouissance. Right (*droit*) is not duty. Nothing forces anyone to enjoy (*jouir*) except the superego. The superego is the imperative of jouissance - Enjoy!
